What is RAG, actually? Retrieval-Augmented Generation is a way of giving a language model access to specific, current information before it answers a question, instead of relying only on what it learned during training. When a user asks something, the system first searches a knowledge base, such as internal documents, product data, or policy records, for the most relevant pieces of information. Those pieces are then handed to the language model along with the original question, so the model generates its answer grounded in that retrieved content rather than guessing from memory. This is what allows an AI system to answer accurately about things that didn't exist when it was trained, like last week's pricing update or a client's private records. Where this matters in practice: - Customer support assistants that must reflect current policies, not outdated ones - Internal tools answering questions against proprietary company documents - The misconception that a bigger model alone fixes factual accuracy - A system that cites its sources and declines when retrieval finds nothing relevant A language model without retrieval is reasoning from memory. A language model with retrieval is reasoning from evidence, and for any business where a wrong answer carries real cost, that difference is the entire point. posts.title: RAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Enterprise AI | Rajendra Akuthota posted on the topic | LinkedIn
posts.content:
RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) is one of the most practical uses of Generative AI today. Companies want AI to answer questions using **their own trusted business data**, not just the LLM’s general knowledge. This data can include internal documents, policies, databases, knowledge bases, support tickets, runbooks, and project documentation. **How does RAG work?** **1. Ingest** → Collect enterprise data **2. Transform** → Clean and split it into chunks **3. Store** → Create embeddings and store them in a vector database **4. Retrieve** → Find the most relevant information for the user's question **5. Generate** → Give that context to the LLM to generate an accurate answer **Simple example:** Employee asks: “How do I reset my company password?” RAG retrieves the company’s password-reset policy → sends the relevant information to the LLM → generates an answer based on the company’s actual policy. RAG can be used for **enterprise search, customer support, HR assistants, technical support, analytics copilots, and developer assistants.** For Data Professionals moving into **Generative AI**, RAG is a great architecture to understand.
One enterprise wrinkle is that “trusted business data” isn’t automatically trusted just because it came from an internal repository. Retrieval needs to answer two different questions: is this relevant, and is this the authoritative version of truth for this question right now? [Rajendra Akuthota](https://www.linkedin.com/in/rajendraakuthota1?trk=public_post_comment-text)
Ontology is what gives AI systems shared meaning. Without it, enterprise data can look like a maze of table names, cryptic columns, hidden joins, and business rules buried inside code. That creates a serious problem for AI. The system may see tbl\_cust, cust\_id, ord\_hdr, and itm\_mstr, but it still has to guess what they mean and how they connect. With ontology, those guesses become explicit definitions. → Entities Customer, Order, Product, Supplier. → Properties Name, status, amount, tier, price. → Relationships Customer places Order. Order contains Product. → Hierarchies A VIP Customer is still a Customer. → Rules Every Order must belong to a Customer. This changes how AI interacts with enterprise data. Instead of relying on disconnected schemas and undocumented conventions, agents can reason over a shared model of the business. That means: → One definition for each concept → Relationships become explicit → Business rules are queryable → AI answers stay grounded in meaning → The same semantic layer can support multiple apps, agents, and analytics systems The biggest benefit is consistency. Without ontology, every new application has to reinterpret the same data. With ontology, people and AI operate from the same business vocabulary. And that is what turns raw enterprise data into something AI systems can actually understand, connect, and reason over.

posts.title: RAG Pipeline: How Retrieval-Augmented Generation Works | Mayank Kumar posted on the topic | LinkedIn
posts.content:
RAG PIPELINE: HOW IT WORKS How do AI systems provide accurate, context-aware answers using your own data? Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) combines information retrieval with Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate answers grounded in relevant external information. 1. Data Ingestion — Collect data from PDFs, documents, websites, APIs, and databases. 2. Data Preprocessing — Clean, normalize, and split content into smaller, manageable chunks. 3. Embedding Generation — Convert text chunks into vector embeddings that capture semantic meaning. 4. Indexing — Store embeddings, text, and metadata in a vector database for efficient searching. 5. Retrieval — Convert the user's query into an embedding and retrieve the most relevant chunks using similarity search. An optional reranker can improve relevance. 6. Generation — Provide the retrieved context to an LLM, which generates a relevant, context-aware answer. Key Takeaway: RAG connects LLMs with external knowledge, helping improve factual accuracy, reduce hallucinations, and provide answers based on your data. However, its reliability still depends on the quality of the retrieved information and the model's response. Popular Tools: FAISS, Chroma, Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, and LangChain. Remember: Ingest → Preprocess → Embed → Index → Retrieve → Generate. posts.title: RAG Revolutionizes AI with Retrieval and Generation | Muhammad Usman Shahbaz posted on the topic | LinkedIn
posts.content:
Few people actually understand how RAG works. Most AI apps fail for one simple reason: they don’t know your data. That’s where Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) changes everything. Instead of relying only on what a model was trained on, RAG gives it access to relevant, real-time context before generating a response. Here’s the simple flow: ✅ Indexing → Break documents into chunks and turn them into embeddings ✅ Retrieval → Find the most relevant pieces using semantic search ✅ Augmentation → Combine retrieved context with the user query ✅ Generation → Let the LLM produce a grounded, accurate answer The result? If you're building AI products, this isn’t optional anymore it’s foundational. The real power of AI isn’t just generation. It’s retrieval + generation together.
📌 If youre still building AI with basic RAG, youre missing the architectures that will define the next generation of AI application
📌 If youre building AI apps, learn this: RAG = your backend brain.
📌 The Evolution of RAG Design Patterns in 2026: Naive RAG → Reranking → Multimodal → GraphRAG → Hybrid → Agentic
📌 If your AI doesn’t know something, don’t retrain it retrieve it.
Great breakdown. One thing I'd add from the data protection side: the diagram puts PII masking on the query path, but the bigger exposure is often on the indexing side. Once sensitive documents are chunked and embedded, the original access controls and sensitivity labels usually don't come along with them. Without permission-aware retrieval, a RAG app can surface content to users who could never open the source file. Security has to start at step 1, not step 2.
The forward path of a RAG pipeline is well understood by now; the backward path rarely is. The durable advantage is the loop that traces a failed answer to a chunking or ranking decision, decides who may change those settings, and confirms the fix before it reaches every user at once.
RAG helps connect a model’s language capabilities with an organization’s actual knowledge. But the quality of the answer still depends heavily on retrieving the right context in the first place.
The real challenge is retrieval quality chunking, ranking, and source freshness determine whether RAG provides useful evidence or simply generates plausible answers.
The pipeline is foundational, but production RAG needs a feedback loop. Like for example here: Documents change, embeddings become stale, and permissions must survive every retrieval step. I love to add incremental re-indexing, access-control filtering, and versioned evaluations. How do you handle stale or updated documents without rebuilding the entire index?
Very insightful, they it almost covers each step of RAG, And to me Chucking strategy always plays an important role otherwise LLM might be hallucinating with full confidence.

RAG Learning Series: Understanding Retrieval-Augmented Generation As part of my Generative AI learning journey, I'm starting a new series focused on Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) — one of the important techniques for building knowledge-grounded AI applications. 🔍 What is RAG? RAG combines information retrieval with Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate more relevant, context-aware responses using external knowledge sources. 💡 Why do we need RAG? Traditional LLMs have limitations when accessing private data, domain-specific knowledge, and information that wasn't included in their training data. RAG helps address these challenges by retrieving relevant information before generating a response. ⚙️ How does RAG work? 1️⃣ Retrieve — Find relevant information from a knowledge source. 2️⃣ Augment — Add the retrieved context to the user's query. 3️⃣ Generate — Use an LLM to produce a context-aware answer. 📌 Real-world applications: - Enterprise knowledge assistants - Document question-answering systems - Customer support chatbots - Research and information retrieval This is just the beginning! In this series, I'll explore different types of RAG, RAG evaluation using RAGAS, and hands-on projects to understand how RAG systems are built in practice. 🚀 Day 124: Tool Calling & Function Calling Today I learned one of the most important concepts in modern LLM application engineering: Tool Calling / Function Calling. An LLM doesn't need to answer every question using only its internal knowledge. Instead, an application can give the model access to external tools such as: 🔹 Calculator 🔹 Web Search 🔹 Database 🔹 RAG 🔹 APIs 🔹 File Search 🔹 Custom Python Functions The basic architecture is: User ↓ LLM API ↓ Tool Decision ↓ Tool Call ↓ Python Function ↓ Tool Result ↓ LLM ↓ Final Answer For example: User: Calculate 125 × 48 LLM: I need the calculator tool. Tool: 125 × 48 = 6000 LLM: The answer is 6000. One important concept I learned today: The LLM does not directly execute the Python function. The LLM generates a structured tool call, and the application executes the corresponding tool and sends the result back to the model. I also learned about: ✅ Tool schemas ✅ Function arguments ✅ Tool descriptions ✅ Tool selection ✅ Tool execution ✅ Tool results ✅ Multiple tools ✅ Tool calling loops ✅ Tool security ✅ Human approval for sensitive tools This connects directly with what I learned in Phase 9 — AI Agents. The architecture is now becoming: LLM ↓ Decision ↓ Tool Calling ↓ Tool Execution ↓ Observation ↓ LLM ↓ Final Answer Today’s key takeaway: Tool Calling is one of the bridges between a basic LLM application and a real AI Agent system. Next, I’ll focus on Token Usage, Rate Limits, Retry, Exponential Backoff, Error Handling and Cost Optimization to make LLM applications more production-ready. posts.title: LLM Tool Use and Function Calling for Real-World Actions | Praveen Pandey posted on the topic | LinkedIn
posts.content:
Tool Use & Function Calling 🚀 **An LLM can generate an impressive answer. But how does it actually do something in the real world**? That's where **Tool Use & Function Callin**g become powerful. An LLM by itself mainly generates tokens. Give it tools, and it can interact with the outside world: 🔎 Search data 📅 Check calendars 💳 Query payments 🗄️ Read databases ✈️ Search flights ⚙️ Execute workflows 🌐 Call APIs 🧠 What is Function Calling? Function calling allows an LLM to dec**ide: “I need this tool to complete the user's re**quest.” Example: “Find me a flight from Delhi to Dubai under ₹25,000.” The LLM can generate a structured tool call: search\_flights(origin="Delhi", destination="Dubai", max\_price=25000) **The application executes the f**unction, receives the result, and gives it back to the LLM. The LLM then generates the final response. ⚙️ Production **Flow User** Request ↓ 🤖 LLM understands intent ↓ 🎯 Selects appropriate tool ↓ 📦 Generates structured argument**s ↓ 🔧 Tool / A**PI executes ↓ 📊 Tool returns result ↓ 🤖 LLM interprets result ↓ 💬 Final response This creates the f**oundation** for AI agents. 🌍 Real-World Example A travel agent could use: ✈️ search\_flights() 🏨 search\_hotels() 🗺️ get\_maps() 📅 check\_calendar() Instead of simply saying: “Here are some possible flights.” The a**gent can actually retrieve live information a**nd perform actions. ⚠️ Common Mistakes ❌ Poor function descriptions ❌ Giving the model too many tools ❌ Not validating tool arguments ❌ No timeout/retry strategy ❌ Ignoring permissions and sensitive data ❌ Returning raw tool errors to users ❌ No fallback when a tool fails 💡 Eng**ineering Insight Tools are th**e hands of your AI. But funct**ion calling is the decision layer that tells thos**e hands what to do. The quality of an agent dep**ends heavily on: Clear tool schemas + Secure execution + Validation + Error handl**ing + Observability More tools don't automatically create **a smarter agent. Better tools + better orchestration =** bett**er AI systems. 🚀 The shift from “AI that answers” to “AI that acts” s**tar**ts with tool use. If you were building an AI agent today, which tool would you give it first: Search, Database, API, Code Execution**, or something else? posts.title: LLMs Designed Backwards: A New Approach to Tool Integration | Aleksandr Volkov posted on the topic | LinkedIn
posts.content:
We may have designed LLM tools backwards. Function calling was an excellent bridge from chat models to software: place schemas in context, receive a structured call, execute it, return the result, and resume. We began treating the bridge as the architecture. The scaling problem is now explicit. Anthropic says a GitHub, Slack, Sentry, Grafana, and Splunk setup can consume about 55,000 tokens in definitions before any work begins, while selection accuracy degrades beyond 30–50 tools. The remedy is tool search and deferred loading: another tool to find the tools the model was previously asked to remember. We encountered this while building an AI concierge. A harness designed for one environment was fast because it knew where its capabilities lived. A universal harness spent time and tokens discovering and loading them. More nominal capability produced more coordination inside the context window. There is a deeper failure mode. A hook may terminate generation, inject a skill, and restart inference without preserving the model’s planning state. Every invocation then becomes a partial reset. The longer the reasoning trajectory, the more state must be reconstructed after each interruption. Heavy reasoning is not inherently worse at tools; a badly designed harness gives it more trajectory to lose. This is harness-induced executive fragmentation. Coding agents point toward a different design. Many obtain substantial leverage from read, edit, and shell. Shell is a meta-effector: the model generates an adapter when needed instead of receiving every schema in advance. Security, permissions, and verification then belong in the runtime. From first principles, a sensor observes relevant state, while an effector produces a constrained, auditable state transition; neither needs to be a permanent API manual in the model’s working memory. An agent runtime could instead combine a small observation-and-action kernel with an external capability registry, just-in-time procedures, execution state outside the transcript, and runtime control of permissions, verification, and cost. A skill then becomes a discoverable, executable procedure loaded when required, not prose the model must remember. The model maintains the task trajectory while the runtime resolves capabilities without repeatedly breaking it. Perhaps LLMs should not “call tools” in the current sense. They should express an intended state transition, its constraints, and the evidence required for completion; the system should decide how to realize it. Tool calling solved the problem of connecting a language model to software. It may not be the right foundation for sustained autonomous work. What would LLM input and output look like if we designed it today from first principles? posts.title: LLM Tool Calling and Function Calling Explained | Samuel Chirala posted on the topic | LinkedIn
posts.content:
🚀 30 Days AI Engineering Challenge | Day 16 Yesterday, we explored AI Agents. Today, let's answer a critical engineering question: 🤔 How does an LLM actually interact with the outside world? Suppose a user asks: "What's the current status of my order?" An LLM by itself doesn't automatically have permission to query your order database. Instead, an application can expose a controlled tool such as: get\_order\_status(order\_id) The model can determine that this tool is relevant and provide the required arguments. The application then executes the function and returns the result to the model. This pattern is commonly called Tool Calling or Function Calling. 📘 Day 16 Topic: Tool Calling & Function Calling – Connecting LLMs to Real-World Systems Today's presentation explores: ✅ What is Tool Calling? ✅ Function Calling vs normal API calls ✅ How an LLM selects a tool ✅ Tool schemas ✅ Arguments and structured inputs ✅ Tool execution ✅ Returning tool results ✅ Multi-tool workflows ✅ Validation and error handling ✅ Authentication and authorization ✅ Human approval ✅ Tool security ✅ Observability ✅ Real-world AI Agent architecture ✅ Interview questions 🧠 Simplified flow User Request ↓ LLM ↓ Select Tool ↓ Generate Structured Arguments ↓ Application Validates Request ↓ Execute Function / API ↓ Tool Result ↓ LLM ↓ Final Response The important architectural principle is: The LLM proposes the action. The application controls the action. That distinction is extremely important. Imagine an Agent has access to: • get\_customer\_profile() • search\_orders() • cancel\_order() • issue\_refund() You don't want the model to have unrestricted authority to execute every operation. The application should enforce: 🔐 Authentication 🔐 Authorization 🔐 Input validation 🔐 Business rules 🔐 Rate limits 🔐 Approval requirements 🔐 Audit logging Example User: "Cancel my order #12345." The model may identify: Tool: cancel\_order Argument: order\_id = 12345 But before the actual operation happens, the application should verify: ✔ User identity ✔ User permission ✔ Order ownership ✔ Cancellation eligibility ✔ Business rules ✔ Whether human approval is required Only then should the operation execute. My biggest takeaway Tool Calling isn't about giving an LLM unlimited access to your application. It's about creating a controlled interface between probabilistic AI and deterministic software systems. That's why Tool Calling is such an important concept for AI Engineers. 🚀 Day 16/30 complete. — Samuel Chirala

posts.title: How function calling works in 4 steps: 1. You define tools with schemas You describe each function: name, purpose, parameters, and types.…
posts.content:
1w
How function calling works in 4 steps: 1. You define tools with schemas You describe each function: name, purpose, parameters, and types. The LLM uses these schemas to decide which tool to call and how. 2. The LLM proposes tool calls When the model needs to act, it returns a function call request with arguments. It never executes code directly. It proposes: "I want to call write_file with these arguments." 3. Your system executes the function You run the function in your code, capture the output (success, error, file content), and send results back to the LLM. This is where the actual action happens. 4. The LLM integrates the results The model processes the output and continues the conversation. It can chain additional tool calls or present the final result to the user. This loop continues until the task is complete. For coding agents, this means: - Reading existing code - Modifying files - Running tests - Checking results - Making adjustments The LLM orchestrates it, and your system executes it. I wrote a complete guide on building a coding agent that creates Django apps using function calling. The difference between a chatbot and an agent comes down to one thing: function calling. A chatbot generates text based on its training. It can't take actions. An agent can invoke tools to perform actions and bring results back into the conversation. Here's a simple example: -> Without function calling: You ask: "Tell me a joke about Alexey" The model generates a joke directly from its training. -> With function calling: You ask: "Tell me a joke" The model sees it has access to a make_joke(name) function. It asks: "What's your name?" You reply: "Alexey" The model calls make_joke("Alexey") Your system executes the function and returns the result. The model presents the joke to you. The LLM never executes code directly. It proposes calls; your system runs them. This is what transforms a chatbot into an agent. For a coding agent, the tools become more powerful: - read_file() to inspect code - write_file() to modify projects - execute_bash_command() to run tests - see_file_tree() to understand structure I recently published a guide on building your own coding agent that creates Django apps from a single prompt. AI coding tools can raise the engineering bar—if they are used to accelerate thinking, not replace it. I use agents where the work is structured, repetitive, or easier to review than to write from scratch: • Boilerplate for a new feature module, component scaffold, or typed API client • Test-case ideas, especially around loading, error, empty, and permission-limited states • Refactoring exploration, such as comparing two ways to split a large component • Repository navigation and summarising unfamiliar code paths • Drafting documentation, migration notes, or pull-request descriptions But some decisions always need human review: • Does the change fit the domain model and module boundaries? • Does the component API prevent invalid states? • Does the implementation preserve accessibility and error recovery? • Are the tests meaningful, or do they only confirm the generated implementation? • Is the added abstraction worth its long-term maintenance cost? For example, an agent can propose a clean React component for an API response. The review still needs to decide whether the data is trusted, how failures are represented, and which layer owns caching and invalidation. The trade-off is simple: accepting generated code immediately is faster in the moment. Reviewing it carefully takes longer. But the engineer who merges the change owns the complexity after the prompt is forgotten. My goal is not more AI-generated code. It is faster delivery with the same—or a higher—quality bar. AI agents can reason. But without memory, they keep starting from zero. A useful AI Agent Memory system can be understood in a few simple parts: **User** **Input** → **Retrieve** **Memory** → **Agent** **Reasoning** → **Action** → **Update** **Memory** Here are the main types: 🧠 **1**. **Working** **Memory** Keeps information needed for the current task, like recent messages, tool results, and intermediate steps. 💬 **2**. **Short**-**Term** **Memory** Keeps recent interactions so the agent can continue a conversation or workflow without losing context. 📚 **3**. **Long**-**Term** **Memory** Stores useful information across sessions, such as preferences, facts, and previous decisions. 🕒 **4**. **Episodic** **Memory** Stores past experiences: **Task** → **Action** → **Result** → **Learning** 🔗 **5**. **Semantic** **Memory** Stores facts, concepts, and relationships that can be retrieved when needed. But good memory is not about storing everything. The agent also needs to decide: - What should be remembered? - What should be forgotten? - When should memory be retrieved? - Which memory is actually relevant? The key idea is simple: **Memory** **helps** **turn** **stateless** **LLM** **calls** **into** **more** **context**-**aware** **and** **persistent** **AI** **agents**. Which type of agent memory do you find hardest to build well?
Reasoning without memory is intelligence that keeps forgetting what it learned. How do we build agent memory that preserves the right context without creating noise?
Memory is what turns an agent from stateless to truly context-aware. Which is harder in practice: deciding what to store or retrieving the right memory?
The real challenge isn’t just giving AI agents memory—it’s giving them the right memory at the right time. 🧠 Selective retrieval and forgetting may be what truly separates a smart agent from a cluttered one.
Incredible explanation! 💯 I'd definitely vote for Long-Term Memory. Knowing how to retrieve exactly what's relevant without bloating the LLM's context window is the ultimate balancing act.
Retrieval quality may matter more than memory size. The perfect memory is useless if the agent retrieves the wrong context.
Memory adds another important dimension to model selection. Different agent workloads can require different trade offs in reasoning, context handling, and inference efficiency, so there’s rarely a one model fits all approach. A generic AI response is often a symptom of an underspecified problem. When I work with LLMs, I don't just think about the question I'm asking. I think about the environment the answer needs to operate in. 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐱𝐭. What does the model need to know about the system? 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐬. What can't the solution change? 𝐑𝐮𝐥𝐞𝐬. What must the solution always follow? 𝐄𝐱𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐛𝐞𝐡𝐚𝐯𝐢𝐨𝐫. What is already working that the new solution needs to preserve? 𝐄𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐩𝐮𝐭. What does a useful answer actually need to produce? Without those boundaries, an LLM can produce an answer that is technically sound but completely wrong for the situation. That's not necessarily a model failure. Sometimes the problem simply hasn't been defined precisely enough. When building with AI, I think beyond getting the model to produce an answer. 🧠 AI agents are getting smarter, but their memory management is still holding them back. As an AI developer, managing context is critical for building affordable and reliable applications. Researchers at Xiaohongshu recently introduced Self-GC, a new memory management technique for AI agents. Here is how it improves on standard memory algorithms: ● Instead of blindly deleting old logs, Self-GC uses a planner LLM to decide what to fold, mask, or prune. ● When input tokens fill more than 30 percent of the context window, it evaluates the history and optimizes for cost and retention. ● In complex conversations, Self-GC kept necessary details 84.85 percent of the time, while standard methods dropped to 54.55 percent. Treating LLM memory like operating system garbage collection could be the next step in agentic architecture. Read the full technical breakdown here: [https://hubs.la/Q04wy8Lg0](https://www.linkedin.com/redir/redirect?url=https%3A%2F%2Fhubs%2Ela%2FQ04wy8Lg0&urlhash=3TKq&trk=public_post-text)[#DeepLearningAI](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Fdeeplearningai&trk=public_post-text)[#SoftwareEngineering](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Fsoftwareengineering&trk=public_post-text)[#AIAgents](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Faiagents&trk=public_post-text)
Share
Calling it garbage collection undersells the cost. OS GC is deterministic and nearly free, Self-GC spends an LLM call to decide what survives, so every prune adds latency and its own error rate. 84.85 percent retention still means one important detail in six gets rounded off
This is especially relevant for AI interview applications. An interviewer needs to retain the candidate’s earlier answers, identify recurring knowledge gaps, and ask meaningful follow-up questions without carrying every transcript token forward. Selective memory compression could make longer interview sessions both more consistent and more affordable
Founder, incierge | CTO @NemoTek | Building correctable autonomous systems and AI boundaries for agents
1w
Interesting direction. Agent memory management is not only about cost or retention. What gets folded, masked, pruned, or carried forward determines what the agent can later assemble across turns and tools. For enterprise agents, memory policy becomes part of the data boundary.
I’m curious how reliable the agent is at deciding what information can actually be discarded without affecting future tasks.
Semantic garbage collection (folding, masking, pruning) is a huge upgrade over blunt context window truncation. As context windows grow, managing attention degradation and token cost matters just as much as raw capacity. Really promising direction for agentic systems!
Self-GC's planner LLM is a neat idea - I've seen selective pruning shave roughly 20 % off token usage in production. The extra LLM call bumps latency and can spike costs, so we usually revert to rule-based pruning on the high-throughput routes. What tricks do you use to keep the planner overhead in check for real-time workloads?
More context isn’t necessarily better context. As agents become long-running, intelligently deciding what to retain and what to discard will be critical for both reliability and cost.
That's a really interesting point. We cannot have systems with infinitely large memories. Perhaps new compression techniques could be explored too? This could have huge implications for all storage solutions. Exciting stuff!
Treating agent memory like garbage collection is the right framing, and telling that it came from a production team, not a lab. Context failures look like model failures in the logs, so most teams misdiagnose them and just pay for bigger context windows.
Great insightful post 💎👏

posts.content:
Day 35/50 of [#50DaysOfAI](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2F50daysofai&trk=public_post-text) 🚀 Halfway through the challenge. Today I focused on AI Agent Memory and State — because an agent that forgets everything after every interaction isn’t really useful for complex workflows. What I learned today: 🧠 Short-term memory: Keeping track of the current conversation, task, and intermediate results. 💾 Long-term memory: Persisting useful information across different sessions. 🔄 State management: Tracking where an agent is in a multi-step workflow. 📚 Context management: Deciding what information the model actually needs instead of dumping everything into the context window. 🔎 Memory retrieval: Searching stored information and bringing only the relevant memories back into the current task. 🧹 Memory isn’t storage: Saving everything isn’t intelligence. The system needs to decide what is useful, what is temporary, and what should be forgotten. I built a small agent workflow that maintains state across multiple steps instead of treating every request as an isolated interaction. The architecture became: User → Agent → Retrieve Context → Reason → Tool → Update State → Store Useful Memory → Continue The biggest lesson today: Context is a resource. Give an agent too little context and it won’t understand the task. Give it everything and you increase noise, cost, latency, and the chance of confusing the model. Good AI systems aren’t just about having a huge context window. They’re about selecting the right context at the right moment. 35 days in. 70% of the challenge completed. 15 days left. The goal is no longer just to understand AI concepts. I’m learning how to architect systems that can actually use them. 🧠🔥 [#AIAgents](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Faiagents&trk=public_post-text) [#AgentMemory](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Fagentmemory&trk=public_post-text) [#LLM](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Fllm&trk=public_post-text) [#AIEngineering](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Faiengineering&trk=public_post-text) [#GenerativeAI](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Fgenerativeai&trk=public_post-text) [#MachineLearning](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Fmachinelearning&trk=public_post-text) [#ContextEngineering](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Fcontextengineering&trk=public_post-text) [#Python](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Fpython&trk=public_post-text) [#LearningInPublic](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Flearninginpublic&trk=public_post-text) [#50DaysOfAI](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2F50daysofai&trk=public_post-text)
**High-Level vs Low-Level Agent Building** While learning AI Agents with LangChain, I started to understand an important difference between initialize\_agent and **LangGraph**. 🔹 **initialize\_agent → High-Level** You give the framework the LLM and tools, and it handles most of the Agent orchestration for you. agent = initialize\_agent( tools, llm, agent="zero-shot-react-description" ) You don't need to manually define the Agent loop, tool execution, or routing. 🔹 **LangGraph → Low-Level** With LangGraph, you work with the building blocks directly: State ↓ LLM Node ↓ Decision ↓ Tool Node ↓ LLM Node ↓ ... You explicitly define: State Nodes Tools Conditional edges Routing Loops End conditions So, in simple terms: **initialize\_agent = High-Level → "Build the Agent for me."** **LangGraph = Low-Level → "Give me the building blocks; I'll build the Agent workflow."** For me, understanding this difference is important because I don't just want to **use AI Agents** — I want to understand what is happening **under the hood**. Still learning. Still building. 🚀 [#GenerativeAI](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Fgenerativeai&trk=public_post-text) [#AIAgents](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Faiagents&trk=public_post-text) [#LangChain](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Flangchain&trk=public_post-text) [#LangGraph](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Flanggraph&trk=public_post-text) [#AgenticAI](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Fagenticai&trk=public_post-text) [#LLM](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Fllm&trk=public_post-text) [#Python](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Fpython&trk=public_post-text)

posts.content:
Founder @ SwirlAI • Ex-CPO @ neptune.ai (Acquired by OpenAI) • UpSkilling the Next Generation of AI Talent • Author of SwirlAI Newsletter • Public Speaker
3w
𝗔𝗜 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁’𝘀 𝗠𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆 is the most important piece of 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝘅𝘁 𝗘𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴, this is how we define it 👇 In general, the memory for an agent is something that we provide via context in the prompt passed to LLM that helps the agent to better plan and react given past interactions or data not immediately available. It is useful to group the memory into four types: 𝟭. 𝗘𝗽𝗶𝘀𝗼𝗱𝗶𝗰 - This type of memory contains past interactions and actions performed by the agent. After an action is taken, the application controlling the agent would store the action in some kind of persistent storage so that it can be retrieved later if needed. A good example would be using a vector Database to store semantic meaning of the interactions. 𝟮. 𝗦𝗲𝗺𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗰 - Any external information that is available to the agent and any knowledge the agent should have about itself. You can think of this as a context similar to one used in RAG applications. It can be internal knowledge only available to the agent or a grounding context to isolate part of the internet scale data for more accurate answers. 𝟯. 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗰𝗲𝗱𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗹 - This is systemic information like the structure of the System Prompt, available tools, guardrails etc. It will usually be stored in Git, Prompt and Tool Registries. 𝟰. Occasionally, the agent application would pull information from long-term memory and store it locally if it is needed for the task at hand. 𝟱. All of the information pulled together from the long-term or stored in local memory is called short-term or working memory. Compiling all of it into a prompt will produce the prompt to be passed to the LLM and it will provide further actions to be taken by the system. We usually label 1. - 3. as Long-Term memory and 5. as Short-Term memory. Learn how to think about memory from fundamental principles in my End-to-End AI Engineering Bootcamp (next cohort kicking off mid-October): [https://lnkd.in/dagWE5r3](https://www.linkedin.com/redir/redirect?url=https%3A%2F%2Flnkd%2Ein%2FdagWE5r3&urlhash=hNrl&trk=public_post-text) And that is it! The rest is all about how you architect the topology of your Agentic Systems. Any war stories you have while managing Agent’s memory? Let me know in the comments 👇
Share
Episodic memory is the one that bites teams in practice, since vector retrieval on past interactions often surfaces stale or contradictory actions once the agent has run for weeks. Ranking by recency plus relevance, not just similarity, usually fixes it.
The procedural memory part is the one teams underrate. If the tool list or guardrails drift, the agent looks "forgetful" when the real bug is stale system context.
An agent with tools but no memory is powerful for one task. An agent with memory becomes useful across time. The real engineering challenge is knowing what to remember and what to forget.
Storyteller | Data Architect | Building Scalable Data & AI Foundations for Enterprise Performance | Linkedin Top Voice 2025,2024 | Open to collaboration
3w
Focusing on the fundamental aspect of Context engineering is crucial to understand how memory helps to enahnce the capabilities! [Aurimas Griciūnas](https://lt.linkedin.com/in/aurimas-griciunas?trk=public_post_comment-text)
Agent memory is becoming very interesting for LLM based systems. How do you decide what should stay in long-term memory vs what should be kept only in the current context?
Episodic memory is where many agent systems struggle. Similarity-based retrieval can surface outdated experiences, while ranking by both recency and relevance helps keep memories useful and accurate.
The episodic versus semantic split is the distinction most people flatten into just "give it a vector db". Treating procedural memory as its own layer, tools, guardrails, system prompt structure, explains a lot of the "agent got dumber after we changed one prompt" incidents that don't look like memory bugs on the surface. Which of the four layers tends to break first once an agent moves from demo to real usage?
Great breakdown. The distinction between episodic, semantic, procedural, and working memory makes the architecture much clearer. The real advantage isn’t simply giving agents more memory—it’s giving them the right context, with the right freshness and relevance, at the right moment. That’s what makes agentic systems reliable at scale.
This is an important distinction because agent memory is not about storing everything, it is about retrieving the right context at the right time. The real engineering challenge is designing what should become persistent memory, what belongs in the current context window, and how to avoid irrelevant or outdated information affecting agent behavior. Good memory architecture is ultimately about improving decision quality, not just increasing the amount of information available to the model.
The four-type split maps cleanly to storage decisions, but the harder call in production is eviction. Episodic memory grows linearly with usage and starts poisoning retrieval before anyone notices token cost. Do you evict by recency, by relevance decay, or leave it to the LLM to weight down old context in-prompt?

Every AI agent needs to remember what it's doing, what it's learned and what comes next. Now multiply that across thousands of agents working simultaneously in a data center. As agentic AI scales, the need for memory is growing rapidly. Our team explored how this shift is changing AI infrastructure and found that memory capacity can play a much larger role in inference performance than many realize, especially for long-context workloads. The result? More memory can help AI systems respond faster and handle increasingly complex tasks. That's why we're advancing solutions like our SOCAMM2 modules built with leading-edge low-power DRAM, helping create the memory foundation for the next generation of AI. Read more → [https://bit.ly/3S2fhof](https://www.linkedin.com/redir/redirect?url=https%3A%2F%2Fbit%2Ely%2F3S2fhof&urlhash=B44f&trk=public_post-text)
The real constraint hiding in plain sight: per-agent memory cost compounds faster than per-agent compute. Data centers building for this asymmetry first will reset infrastructure economics. That asymmetry is reshaping infrastructure roadmaps. [Sudharshan Vazhkudai](https://www.linkedin.com/in/sudharshan-vazhkudai-1569733?trk=public_post_comment-text), [Sujit S.](https://www.linkedin.com/in/sujitsomandepalli?trk=public_post_comment-text), [Rajendra Narasimhan](https://www.linkedin.com/in/rajendra-narasimhan-ab45215?trk=public_post_comment-text), and [Micron Technology](https://www.linkedin.com/company/micron-technology?trk=public_post_comment-text) are mapping this right.
While expanding DRAM capacity addresses the growing state and context footprint of agentic workflows,, the deeper architectural challenge is keeping CPU, memory, and orchestration layers balanced as concurrency scales. Managing runtime behavior across thousands of concurrent agent environments will be an important part of sustaining predictable system performance under load.
Strong focus. Scaling agentic AI inevitably shifts the bottleneck from raw compute to memory architecture. Without breakthroughs here, efficient concurrent multi-agent workloads with long contexts would remain a major wall. Great to see the industry tackling this challenge at the hardware level.
The part that surprises teams is how much of a long context is re-read rather than newly generated. An agent revisiting the same files and transcripts across a multi step task pays memory bandwidth over and over, so capacity and locality end up shaping tail latency more than raw compute does. Multiply that across thousands of concurrent agents and the scheduling problem starts to look more like a memory problem than a GPU problem. Does the SOCAMM2 work show a larger gain on long context inference than on batch throughput?
You’re pointing out a key limit in scalable AI, and it’s refreshing to hear practical memory focus. SOCAMM2 could really boost long-context performance.

posts.title: AI Agent Memory Types: Semantic Episodic Procedural In-Context
posts.content:
We often discuss how AI agents plan, reason, and use tools
But their ability to work consistently also depends on how memory is designed👇
An AI agent can use four distinct types of memory
1️⃣ Semantic memory: what does the agent know?
This memory contains facts, definitions, concepts, and relationships that are not tied to one specific event
For an enterprise agent, this could include product information, business terminology, policies, or domain knowledge
2️⃣ Episodic memory: what happened before?
Episodic memory contains past interactions, actions, and outcomes connected to a particular time or situation
It allows the agent to retrieve relevant experience, such as what a user previously requested or how a similar task was handled
3️⃣ Procedural memory: how should the agent behave?
Procedural memory contains the instructions, rules, and skills that guide the agent’s behavior
It can influence how the agent selects tools, follows a workflow, formats a response, or handles an exception
4️⃣ In-context memory: what is active now?
This corresponds to the working information available during the current model call
It can contain the user’s query, recent conversation, retrieved knowledge, relevant past events, instructions, and tool results
Here is how they work together
→ A user submits a query, which enters the active context
→ Procedural memory guides how the agent should approach the task. The agent retrieves factual knowledge from semantic memory and relevant experiences from episodic memory when needed
→ That information returns to the active context, where the agent uses it to generate a response or take an action
It is important to note that not every query requires every memory type
The real challenge is selecting the right memory for the current task and placing the most useful information in the agent’s context
Which of these four memory types is the hardest to implement reliably in your AI agents?
♻️ Repost if you found this useful 💚
For teams deploying agents in production: which memory type has been the most challenging to design well, semantic, episodic, procedural, or in-context, and why?
🧠 AI Concept of the Day: What is Graph RAG?
We’ve already talked about RAG.
But what if the information you need isn't just a collection of documents?
What if the important part is the relationship between the information?
That’s where Graph RAG comes in.
🔍 What is Graph RAG?
Traditional RAG retrieves relevant pieces of text from a knowledge base and gives them to the LLM.
Graph RAG adds a knowledge graph to the process.
Instead of only storing:
Document → Chunk → Embedding
we can represent information as:
Entity → Relationship → Entity
For example:
Customer → purchased → Product
Employee → works for → Company
Doctor → treats → Patient
The AI can then reason using both the information and the relationships between entities.
🤖 Why is this useful?
Imagine asking:
«“Which customers are affected by the product issue reported by our engineering team?”»
A basic RAG system might retrieve documents containing those keywords.
A Graph RAG system can potentially follow relationships across:
Issue → Product → Customers → Support Tickets
This makes it particularly useful when questions require connecting multiple pieces of information.
📚 Where can Graph RAG help?
It can be valuable for:
🏢 Enterprise knowledge bases
💳 Financial analysis
🏥 Healthcare information
🔬 Research
🛒 Recommendation systems
🛠️ Complex troubleshooting
⚔️ RAG vs Graph RAG
Traditional RAG:
“Find information relevant to my question.”
Graph RAG:
“Find information and understand how the pieces are connected.”
Neither is automatically better.
The right approach depends on the type of data and questions your application needs to answer.
💡 My takeaway
Traditional RAG helps AI retrieve knowledge.
Graph RAG helps AI navigate relationships within knowledge.
And when questions become more complex, sometimes knowing how things are connected is just as important as knowing what they are.
\*\*AI doesn't just need knowledge.
Sometimes, it needs a map of that knowledge.\*\* 🧠🕸️

Code can be correct and still fail at scale.
An algorithm may feel fast with 100 records, then become painfully slow when the input grows to one million.
That is exactly what Big-O notation helps us understand.
It describes how an algorithm’s time or space requirements grow as the input size increases.
Here are seven complexities every developer should know:
→ O(1): Constant time
Performance stays roughly the same regardless of input size. Examples include array index access and hash map lookup.
→ O(log n): Logarithmic time
The problem becomes smaller with each operation. Binary search is the classic example.
→ O(n): Linear time
Runtime grows directly with the input. Think array traversal or linear search.
→ O(n log n): Linearithmic time
Common in efficient sorting algorithms such as merge sort and heap sort.
→ O(n²): Quadratic time
Often appears with nested loops, pair comparisons, bubble sort, and selection sort.
→ O(2ⁿ): Exponential time
Runtime can double with every new input. Recursive subset generation is a common example.
→ O(n!): Factorial time
Explores possible permutations and becomes impractical extremely quickly.
The typical growth order is:
O(1) → O(log n) → O(n) → O(n log n) → O(n²) → O(2ⁿ) → O(n!)
Big-O is not about predicting exact execution time.
It helps compare approaches, identify potential bottlenecks, and make better decisions before scale exposes the problem.

"Make it exist first, make it good later" was the golden rule of SaaS. In the AI era, applying it blindly is a recipe for architectural collapse.
In traditional software, a quick prototype is usually just messy code wrapping deterministic logic. You can refactor the backend, swap the database, or clean up technical debt without rewriting the core product value.
AI does not work that way. When teams are pressured to rush out a quick proof-of-concept without foundational diligence, they aren't creating a baseline—they are accumulating compound risk.
The AI Prototyping Trap:
Rushing to "just get an AI feature working" ignores the critical pillars that dictate whether an AI system can actually survive production:
\* Reliability & Hallucination Drift: A prompt wrapper that works 8 times out of 10 in a demo will fail spectacularly at 10,000 requests a day. You cannot "patch" non-deterministic failure modes with simple code refactoring.
\* Scalability & Latency Economics: Building without understanding compute costs, token economics, caching strategies, and context window limits turns a functional demo into an unsustainable balance sheet liability.
\* Data Lineage & Risk Governance: Deploying models without evaluating bias, edge-case safety, data leakage, and compliance constraints creates liabilities that become exponentially harder to unwind post-launch.
\* Methodology Alignment: Jumping straight to fine-tuning or complex multi-agent orchestration when simple deterministic logic or basic retrieval (RAG) was needed creates unnecessary architectural bloat.
Velocity vs. Direction:
A long-term AI vision cannot be achieved with a quick flick of a demo. Moving fast in the wrong architectural direction doesn't get you closer to the goal—it just gets you lost faster.
The path forward isn't moving slowly; it is moving deliberately:
\* Validate Feasibility First: Establish clear benchmarks, baseline evaluations, and risk models before building user-facing layers.
\* Design for Non-Determinism: Architect fallback systems, human-in-the-loop controls, and observability from day zero.
\* Build the Foundation, Not Just the Demo: Treat data quality, evaluation frameworks, and latency budgets as primary features, not post-launch cleanups.
A prototype proves what is flashy; an architecture proves what is viable. If the foundation isn't sound, making it "exist" only accelerates how fast it fails.
If your team faces same challenges when transitioning AI systems from quick PoCs into enterprise-grade production, DM me, let's discuss it to improve it.

posts.title: LLM Gateway Simplifies Multi-Model Integration and Management | Ankesh Kumar posted on the topic | LinkedIn
posts.content:
I’ve definitely been frustrated dealing with different SDKs, APIs, and syntax for every LLM provider. It gets even harder when an agentic system moves from prototype to production. You need to handle LLM routing, provider failures, cost tracking, caching, and observability at scale. This is where an 𝗟𝗟𝗠 𝗚𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘄𝗮𝘆 starts to make sense. The basic architecture is: Application → LLM Gateway → OpenAI / Anthropic / Gemini / Groq / etc. Instead of every application integrating with every provider separately, the gateway provides a unified interface and adds capabilities around LLM calls. I recently explored these capabilities using [LiteLLM AI Gateway](https://www.linkedin.com/company/litellm?trk=public_post-text): 1. Unified API Different providers have different APIs and SDKs. LiteLLM gives you a common completion() interface, so switching providers can be as simple as changing the model string. 2. Automatic Fallbacks What happens when the primary model fails? You can define: Primary → Backup → Another Backup I tested this by intentionally using an invalid model and letting LiteLLM fall back automatically. The application still received a response. 3. Cost Tracking LLM usage means token usage, which means cost. LiteLLM can expose input tokens, output tokens and the estimated cost of individual calls. 4. Caching Why make the same LLM request twice? I tested local caching: the cached response was dramatically faster and avoided another model call. 5. Smart Routing Not every task needs the same model. For example: → Coding → stronger model → Summarization → cheaper model → General queries → faster model The application can use logical model aliases while the router decides which deployment handles the request. 6. Load Balancing Multiple deployments can sit behind the same model alias. The router can distribute requests using strategies such as: → Simple shuffle → Least-busy routing → Latency-based routing 7. Observability The response alone isn't enough. I added callbacks to track: → Model → Prompt → Input/output tokens → Latency → Cost → User This creates a per-call audit trail for debugging and attribution. 8. Task-Aware Routing I also combined these ideas into a small chatbot: User query → classify task → select model → fallback if needed → return response → track latency + cost So coding, summary and general queries can take different model paths. 9. Guardrails The gateway can also act as a control point before a request reaches the LLM. I experimented with: → PII redaction → Prompt-injection detection → Forbidden-topic filtering For example, sensitive information can be detected and replaced before the request is sent to the model. The biggest takeaway for me: once you start using multiple models, an LLM Gateway gives you one place to control the flow: routing, fallbacks, caching, costs, observability, and guardrails [#GenAI](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Fgenai&trk=public_post-text) [#LLM](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Fllm&trk=public_post-text) [#LLMGateway](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Fllmgateway&trk=public_post-text) [#LiteLLM](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Flitellm&trk=public_post-text) [#MLOps](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Fmlops&trk=public_post-text) [#AgenticAI](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Fagenticai&trk=public_post-text) [#AIEngineering](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Faiengineering&trk=public_post-text) [#GenerativeAI](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Fgenerativeai&trk=public_post-text)
Really clean breakdown, Ankesh. One nuance worth separating: the gateway response cache you tested only helps when a request repeats, but provider-side prompt caching reuses the KV of a stable prefix even when the full request differs - so it pays off on agent loops that never repeat exactly. The catch is it's prefix-strict: ProjectDiscovery sat at a 7% hit rate because working memory lived inside their system prompt and invalidated it every step; moving it to the end got them to 84% and cut LLM cost 59%. Are you leaning on the gateway cache, or passing through the provider's prompt cache too?

posts.content:
🚀 The LLM Gateway: The Missing Abstraction Layer in Enterprise AI
As enterprises move from experimenting with GenAI to building production-grade AI platforms, one problem becomes increasingly obvious:
👉 Your application shouldn’t need to know which LLM is running underneath.
Today, an application might directly integrate with Azure OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Bedrock, local models, or open-source inference engines.
That works initially.
But at enterprise scale, it quickly becomes:
❌ Multiple SDKs
❌ Different APIs
❌ Provider-specific logic
❌ No centralized cost control
❌ Fragmented observability
❌ Difficult model switching
❌ Hard-to-manage security & governance
💡 This is where an LLM Gateway becomes powerful.
🧠 The Architecture
With LiteLLM acting as the LLM Gateway, applications get:
🔹 One API → 100+ LLMs
🔹 Smart Routing & Load Balancing
🔹 Automatic Fallbacks & Retries
🔹 Rate Limiting & Budgets
🔹 Centralized Cost Tracking
🔹 Authentication & API Key Management
🔹 Observability & Tracing
🔹 Policies & Guardrails
Your applications simply communicate with the gateway.
The gateway decides where and how the request should be executed.
🏗️ Think of it as an API Gateway for Intelligence
Traditional API Gateway:
Client → API Gateway → Backend Services
LLM Gateway:
AI Application → LLM Gateway → Best Model / Provider
The difference?
The gateway can make decisions based on:
⚡ Latency
💰 Cost
🎯 Model capability
📊 Availability
🔐 Policy
📈 Traffic
🌍 Region
🔄 Provider health
🔥 The Bigger Architectural Benefit
The real value isn’t just supporting multiple LLMs.
It’s decoupling your AI applications from the LLM ecosystem.
Your application depends on:
“I need an LLM capable of performing this task.”
Not:
“I must use Provider X’s model.”
This creates a much more flexible, resilient, and governable AI architecture.
And when a new model arrives tomorrow?
You shouldn’t have to rewrite your applications.
Add the model → configure the gateway → route traffic.
That’s the abstraction enterprises need as the LLM landscape continues to evolve.
💭 One architectural principle I strongly believe in:
Don’t couple your AI applications to a model.
Couple them to an AI capability.
The models will keep changing.
Your architecture shouldn’t have to.
Spent the last few days refactoring our generative AI footprint, and it led to a big realization about where AI system design is heading.
Last year, everyone built LLM integrations straight into application services—direct API keys, custom retry loops, and scattered prompt templates.
Now? That technical debt is catching up fast.
As a Solution Architect, the most critical design pattern I'm implementing right now is the AI Gateway (or LLM Proxy Layer).
If your application services are calling OpenAI, Anthropic, or internal models directly, you’re missing a crucial enterprise control plane.
When you put an AI Gateway between your services and your model endpoints, you instantly solve four massive architectural headaches:
**Token Rate Limiting & Cost Guardrails:** Enforce hard budget caps per application or team before a runaway loop burns £10k overnight.
**Dynamic Fallbacks & Routing:** If primary provider endpoints experience high latency or 5xx errors, automatically failover to a secondary model without touching application code.
**Centralized Security & PII Redaction:** Strip sensitive data, enforce prompt injection guards, and manage virtual API keys in one place instead of auditing 20 microservices.
**Unified Telemetry:** Track Time-To-First-Token (TTFT), token consumption, and cost attribution from a single dashboard.
Building with AI isn't just about prompt engineering anymore. It’s about building resilient, cost-aware architecture around probabilistic models.
Are you still calling model APIs directly from app services, or have you shifted to a gateway pattern?
AI ecosystem is no longer a model stack. It is becoming an ecosystem of interconnected capabilities.
One of the things I have been exploring recently is how quickly the architecture around LLMs has expanded.
A few years ago, an AI application could largely be described as:
Application → LLM → Response
Today, a production AI system may involve retrieval, embeddings, agent orchestration, memory, tool connectivity, security controls, observability, automation and multiple model providers.
That changes the architecture question.
It is no longer simply:
“Which LLM should we use?”
The better question is:
“What capabilities does our AI system need, and where should each capability live?”
🔹 LLM provides the reasoning and generation capability.
🔹 RAG & Data connects the model to enterprise knowledge and current information.
🔹 Embeddings provide the semantic representation required to search and retrieve information effectively.
🔹 Agent frameworks introduce planning, state, tool usage and multi-step execution.
🔹 MCP & tool connectivity provide a structured way for AI applications and agents to interact with external tools and data sources.
🔹 AI Security becomes critical as models gain access to data, tools and business actions.
🔹 Observability allows teams to understand what happened across prompts, retrieval, model calls, tool calls, latency, cost and failures.
🔹 Memory enables systems to retain useful context across interactions and workflows.
🔹 AI agent platforms provide the runtime capabilities needed to build and operate agentic applications.
🔹 Automation connects AI reasoning with repeatable business processes and downstream actions.
🔹 Vector databases & search provide the retrieval foundation for many knowledge-intensive AI applications.
The interesting part is that none of these capabilities exists in isolation.
For example:
User → Agent → LLM → Retrieve → Vector Search → Tool/MCP → Business System → Observe → Respond
And as the system becomes more autonomous, the architecture must also answer harder questions:
Who can access what?
Which agent can call which tool?
What data can enter the context?

posts.title: LLM-D Optimizes LLM Inference with Cache-Aware Routing and Prefill/Decode Disaggregation | Isreal Urephu posted on the topic | LinkedIn
posts.content:
I’ve been exploring 𝗹𝗺-𝗱 for a while now, and what interests me most is how it addresses some of the problems I’ve experienced while running inference with vLLM and similar engines.
A typical inference path might look like:
𝗨𝘀𝗲𝗿 → 𝗚𝗹𝗼𝗯𝗮𝗹 𝗔𝗰𝗰𝗲𝗹𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗼𝗿 / 𝗥𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗲 𝟱𝟯 → 𝗥𝗲𝗴𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗟𝗼𝗮𝗱 𝗕𝗮𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗿 → 𝗚𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘄𝗮𝘆 𝗔𝗣𝗜 → 𝗟𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗟𝗟𝗠 / 𝗔𝗜 𝗚𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘄𝗮𝘆 → 𝘃𝗟𝗟𝗠 → 𝗚𝗣𝗨
That works.
But once you start running multiple inference replicas, things get more complicated.
One frustration I’ve had is KV-cache locality.
Each vLLM replica has its own cache state. A normal Kubernetes load balancer or AI gateway may know that a replica is healthy, but it does not necessarily know which replica already has the useful prefix KV cache for a request.
So a request can land on another replica and repeat prefill work unnecessarily.
llm-d adds cache-aware routing through its router/EPP. It can consider signals such as prefix-cache locality and load when selecting an inference replica.
That means fewer unnecessary recomputations and potentially better TTFT.
GPU HBM is limited, so useful KV blocks eventually get evicted.
llm-d supports extending KV-cache capacity into lower-cost tiers such as CPU RAM, local storage and shared storage.
This makes previously computed prefixes more reusable instead of always throwing that work away and recomputing it on the GPU.
Prefill and decode behave very differently.
Prefill is largely compute-bound.
Decode is largely memory-bandwidth-bound.
Running both on the same replicas can create interference, especially with long prompts.
With prefill/decode disaggregation, you can run dedicated prefill and decode pools, scale them independently, and transfer the KV cache between them over a high-speed network such as RoCE or InfiniBand.
It is not trying to replace vLLM, Kubernetes or the AI gateway.
It adds an inference-aware scheduling and routing layer where normal infrastructure load balancing starts to become too generic.
Scaling LLM inference is not just about adding more GPUs. The routing layer needs to understand the workload too.
Nice : )
Why spend $25,000+/month on 8x H100 GPU clusters just to host frontier 70B–320B models?
When only a fraction of experts activate per token, treating GPU VRAM, host DRAM, and NVMe as a unified tiered memory hierarchy fundamentally changes the unit economics of AI inference:
📉 The Business ROI:
We open-sourced Turing Engine (v1.2.0) with complete production serving primitives (OpenAI/Anthropic dual gateway, continuous batching, and sub-50µs AI traffic admission control).
🔗 Explore the project & benchmarks:
Founder & CEO @ Devable | Building growth engines for AI-native devtools & platforms | LLMs, RAG, AI Agents | AI Engineering
Run frontier MoE models on hardware you already own!
Colibrì is a pure C inference engine that runs massive Mixture-of-Experts models by treating VRAM, RAM, and NVMe storage as one memory hierarchy.
The key idea is that MoE models may have hundreds of billions or even trillions of parameters, but only a small subset of experts are activated for each token.
So instead of trying to keep the entire model in GPU memory, Colibrì moves weights across different storage tiers depending on which experts are actually needed.
Hot experts can stay in VRAM or RAM. Colder experts can live on NVMe and get streamed in when the router selects them.
This turns model loading into more of a dynamic placement problem.
Colibrì tracks routing patterns, keeps frequently used experts closer to compute, and can prefetch experts for the next layer before they are requested.
The result is that limited VRAM changes how fast the model runs, not which model you are running.
Key capabilities:
It’s 100% open source.
I've shared the GitHub repo in the comments!
Run frontier MoE models on hardware you already own!
Colibrì is a pure C inference engine that runs massive Mixture-of-Experts models by treating VRAM, RAM, and NVMe storage as one memory hierarchy.
The key idea is that MoE models may have hundreds of billions or even trillions of parameters, but only a small subset of experts are activated for each token.
So instead of trying to keep the entire model in GPU memory, Colibrì moves weights across different storage tiers depending on which experts are actually needed.
Hot experts can stay in VRAM or RAM. Colder experts can live on NVMe and get streamed in when the router selects them.
This turns model loading into more of a dynamic placement problem.
Colibrì tracks routing patterns, keeps frequently used experts closer to compute, and can prefetch experts for the next layer before they are requested.
The result is that limited VRAM changes how fast the model runs, not which model you are running.
Key capabilities:
It’s 100% open source.
I've shared the GitHub repo in the comments!
The biggest LLM serving idea of the last two years is embarrassingly simple: prefill and decode are different workloads, so stop running them on the same GPUs.
Prefill chews through the whole prompt in parallel: giant matmuls, compute-bound, the GPU's tensor cores saturated. Decode emits one token at a time, and each token requires streaming ALL the model weights from memory for a sliver of compute: bandwidth-bound, tensor cores mostly idle. Put both on one GPU and they poison each other. Prefill bursts stall decode streams (latency spikes); decode occupancy steals capacity from prefill (throughput loss). You tune for one metric and the other degrades.
Disaggregated serving splits the fleet. Prefill nodes do nothing but ingest prompts and produce KV caches. Decode nodes do nothing but generate tokens from those caches. Between them, the KV cache ships across a fast interconnect, and paged, block-structured caches make that transfer streamable rather than monolithic.

posts.title: ReAct vs Orchestration: Risk and Reliability in AI Agents - LinkedIn
posts.content:
ReAct and orchestrated agents both get called 'AI agents.' That label is hiding two different bets.
A ReAct agent is one continuous LLM loop — Thought, Action, Observation, repeat. At every step, the model decides what to do next, whether to continue, and when it's done. There is no predefined path.
An orchestrated agent — LangGraph and its equivalents — runs on a graph. Nodes and edges, defined upfront. The LLM decides only what happens inside a node. The sequence between nodes is fixed.
The difference is where the task puts its risk.
ReAct wins when the solution path can't be known in advance — research, debugging, open-ended exploration. You need the model free to change direction based on what it just observed.
Orchestration wins when the steps are already known and only the content varies — approvals, extraction pipelines, triage. Instead of asking the model to find the path. You're asking it to execute one.
Here's what most comparisons miss: **a ReAct agent's reliability compounds multiplicatively across every step, because every step is its own inference call.** A 95% success rate per step leaves you at 46% by step 15. Orchestration leaves the model exactly as smart as it was. What changes is where the probability lives — bounded inside a node, not spread across the whole trajectory. The content of a node is still inferred. The transition to the next node is not, so a failure at step 9 doesn't force you to re-derive steps 1 through 8.
So the real question is how much of the task you're willing to let compound.
If the task's value depends on finishing a long chain reliably, orchestration is the only thing standing between you and multiplying your way to failure.
If anyone wants to go deeper here — this was one of the first courses I took when I started working with agents: [https://learn.deeplearning.ai/courses/ai-agents-in-langgraph](https://learn.deeplearning.ai/courses/ai-agents-in-langgraph?trk=public_post_comment-text)
AI generated 100 test cases. I kept 20.
Not because the rest were wrong.
Because they didn't cover a single new risk.
Here's the misconception I see spreading: more AI-generated tests = better coverage. It doesn't. It means more surface area that looks like coverage but isn't.
I ran an experiment. Gave AI an API spec, business rules, edge case hints. Got back 100+ scenarios - valid inputs, invalid inputs, boundary values, missing fields, response code variations. Impressive on paper.
Then I reviewed each test against one question: what unique failure does this protect against?
That's where the number collapsed.
Multiple tests were triggering the same backend validation rule with different input values. Same code path. Same failure mode. Grouped - I needed one, maybe two.
Others were boundary variations already covered at a lower level.
Some were technically valid scenarios with near-zero production risk.
The 20 I kept weren't better written. They represented different ways the system could actually fail.
AI is fast at breadth. It'll generate every obvious combination from the spec you give it. That's genuinely useful - as a starting point.
What it won't do reliably: decide which parts of that surface deserve your attention. Concurrency issues. State accumulated across calls. Partial failures. Business assumptions that live in someone's head, not in the spec.
That prioritization is still engineering work.
More tests are not free. They cost execution time, maintenance, debugging, and noise. A suite of 100 redundant tests gives you false confidence and real overhead.
AI made test generation cheap. It didn't make test maintenance free.
If every test in your AI-generated suite had to justify which unique risk it covers - how many would survive?
This is how you get an AI agent to improve its own output, without you re-prompting it every single time.
If you keep re-prompting an agent because the output isn't good enough yet, you are being the loop.
There is a pattern that takes you out of it, and one condition largely decides whether it works.
It's an agent-loop pattern.
The workflow runs, an evaluation step checks the output, and makes one of two decisions:
Ship it, or run another iteration.
Each pass can take the previous output and the evaluator's feedback, improve it, then submit it for evaluation again.
Whether this is powerful or useless comes down to the quality of that check.
The strongest quality gates are measurable and automatable.
If you can write a deterministic test that decides whether the output is good enough, the architecture gets very clean.
Refactoring behind a test suite is the obvious case.
So is research with explicit coverage requirements, where each pass has a defined gap it needs to close.
But the gate does not literally have to be code.
An LLM evaluator can also score things like completeness, tone, clarity, or adherence to a rubric.
The important question is whether the system can evaluate the result reliably enough without you stepping back into the loop.
If your gate is just "I'll know it when I see it," you don't have much of a gate.
You have a preference.
And a loop trying to optimize against a vague preference can declare victory early, oscillate, or keep spinning.
When iterative feedback is unreliable but you can rank finished outputs, use a different shape.
Generate multiple candidates in parallel, then use an evaluator to score or rank them and keep the best.
That terminates by construction instead of waiting for a refinement loop to converge.
Then bound it.
A loop whose stopping condition might never pass needs a ceiling on iterations, cost, or both.
I cap mine, and I treat hitting the cap as a signal that the generator, evaluator, or criteria need attention rather than automatically raising the cap.
The question I would use is:
Can the system reliably decide whether another iteration is needed?

🤖 What actually makes an AI system an “agent”? A big part of the answer is the ReAct loop: 🧠 Reason — Determine what information is needed ⚙️ Act — Call the appropriate tool or API 👀 Observe — Analyze the result and decide what to do next 🔁 Repeat — Continue until there is enough information to answer Unlike basic tool calling, a ReAct agent doesn’t always plan every action upfront. It can use the result of one tool call to determine whether another action is needed—making the workflow more adaptive and efficient. This becomes even more powerful when combined with Qdrant 🚀 Qdrant can serve as the agent’s long-term knowledge layer by retrieving semantically relevant documents, previous interactions, or application context. Each retrieved result becomes a new observation that helps the agent decide its next step. A practical flow might look like: 🔎 Search Qdrant for relevant context 🧠 Reason over the retrieved information 🛠️ Call another tool if necessary 👀 Observe the result ✅ Generate a grounded final response Key takeaway: building effective agents isn't just about adding more tools. It is about controlling when tools are called, how observations influence decisions, and when the loop should stop—especially since every additional step can increase latency and cost. 📚 Great resource for understanding the ReAct loop with a practical example: [https://lnkd.in/gSddbTNY](https://www.linkedin.com/redir/redirect?url=https%3A%2F%2Flnkd%2Ein%2FgSddbTNY&urlhash=Wvcp&trk=public_post-text) 💬 What do you think is the biggest challenge when building ReAct agents: retrieval quality, tool reliability, cost, latency, or preventing endless loops?
