posts.title: ReAct Pattern for Autonomous LLM Agents - LinkedIn
posts.content:
Most LLM applications stop at generating text.
Agents need to do something with the world.
That's where the ReAct pattern becomes important.
ReAct = Reason + Act
Instead of:
Prompt → LLM → Answer
A ReAct agent works more like:
Reason → Act → Observe → Reason → Act → Observe → Answer
The key idea is the feedback loop.
A simple example
Suppose you ask an agent:
«“What is the current stock price of X, and how much has it changed this week?”»
The agent might:
1️⃣ Reason
“I need current market data.”
↓
2️⃣ Act
Call a stock-price API.
↓
3️⃣ Observe
"Current price = $185"
↓
4️⃣ Reason
“I also need the price from 7 days ago.”
↓
5️⃣ Act
Call the historical-price API.
↓
6️⃣ Observe
"Price 7 days ago = $175"
↓
7️⃣ Reason
“That's approximately a 5.7% increase.”
↓
8️⃣ Answer
Return the result to the user.
So, is ReAct just tool calling?
Not exactly.
Tool calling answers:
«“Which tool should I use?”»
ReAct adds:
«“What should I do next based on what I just observed?”»
That's the important distinction.
The agent isn't blindly following a predefined sequence.
It can use the result of one action to determine its next action.
The mental model
Traditional LLM
"Input → LLM → Output"
LLM + Tools
"Input → LLM → Tool → Output"
ReAct Agent
"Input"
↓
Reason
↓
Act
↓
Observe
↓
Reason
↓
Act
↓
Observe
↓
Final Answer
This makes ReAct useful for:
More autonomy also means more failure modes.
An uncontrolled agent can cause:
Latency ↑
Token usage ↑
Tool calls ↑
Cost ↑
Failure probability ↑
So production agents need guardrails:
→ Maximum iterations
→ Timeouts
→ Tool permissions
→ Input/output validation
→ Error handling
→ State management
→ Fallback strategies
Agentic AI isn't just about giving an LLM more tools.
It's about designing a reliable closed-loop system around the model.
The real principle behind ReAct is simple:
Think → Act → Observe → Adapt → Repeat
Once you understand this loop, many modern agent architectures become much easier to understand.
And that's also why frameworks like LangGraph are useful: they give us explicit control over these loops, states, transitions, and failure paths.
The model provides the intelligence.
The architecture provides the control.
That's where real agent engineering begins.
𝐈 𝐰𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐫𝐞𝐞 𝐰𝐞𝐞𝐤𝐬 𝐞𝐯𝐚𝐥𝐮𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐨𝐨𝐥𝐬 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐰𝐫𝐨𝐧𝐠 𝐥𝐚𝐲𝐞𝐫.
Needed better retrieval for our RAG system. Spent those weeks comparing agent frameworks — LangChain vs CrewAI vs AutoGen. Built prototypes. Ran benchmarks. Wrote a recommendation doc.
Then a colleague said: "Your retrieval is bad because your vector database isn't filtering properly. That's layer 3, not layer 2."
She was right. Swapped our vector search config. Retrieval improved immediately. The agent framework was never the problem.
Here's the map:
Layer 1: Model Providers
Claude, OpenAI, Gemini, LLaMA, Mistral, Grok, DeepSeek, Cohere. The models everything else sits on. Treat this layer as swappable from day one. It's the fastest-moving row on the board and the easiest to get locked into. The team that hardcodes one provider regrets it within six months.
Layer 2: Application Frameworks
LangChain, LlamaIndex, Haystack, DSPy, Guardrails AI. Build full-stack LLM apps with memory, chains, and tools. DSPy and Guardrails represent a different school of thought — one optimizes prompts programmatically, the other constrains outputs. Worth understanding the philosophy before you pick.
Layer 3: Vector Databases
FAISS, ChromaDB, Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, Milvus, Redis. Store embeddings for RAG and semantic search. The real choice is operational, not algorithmic. Self-hosted vs managed shapes your architecture more than recall benchmarks ever will.
Layer 4: Prompt Engineering Tools
PromptLayer, Langfuse, ChainForge, PromptPerfect, PromptTools. Version, evaluate, and manage prompts. The layer teams skip and then regret. Prompts in production without versioning and evaluation are untested code running in front of users.
Layer 5: Agent and Multi-Agent Systems
AutoGen, CrewAI, LangGraph, AutoGPT, CAMEL-AI, Manus. Orchestrate tasks, agents, memory, and planning. Multi-agent is genuinely powerful and genuinely overprescribed. Try one agent with good tools before you build a committee.
Layer 6: No-Code and Low-Code
Flowise, Langflow, n8n, Cursor, Replit, Chatbase. Build LLM apps without heavy engineering. The fastest way to validate an idea before anyone commits real development time.
How do you know which layer your problem lives in?
You don't need all six layers. You need to know which one your problem lives in.
Which layer are you stuck in right now?
What if the biggest RAG problem isn't the tool?
The layer-based diagnosis is the part I find most useful here.
I’d take it one step further for production systems: \*\*don't just identify the layer — instrument it.\*\*
For a RAG pipeline, you can trace:
Query → Retrieval → Reranking → Context → Generation → Output
If you measure each stage independently, a poor answer becomes a diagnosable engineering problem instead of a reason to replace the entire stack.
That’s where observability and evaluation become critical. You need to know whether you're dealing with a retrieval problem, context problem, model problem, or orchestration problem before introducing more complexity.
\*\*Diagnose → measure → optimize → then change the architecture.\*\*
Otherwise, it's very easy to solve the wrong problem with a better tool.

🧠 What even IS an AI Agent?
It's not just a chatbot that answers questions.
An AI Agent thinks, decides which tool to use, executes it, reads the result, and loops until it has a real answer.
That loop has a name: ReAct (Reason + Act). And once you understand it, everything clicks.
The pipeline that makes it work:
① Environment & Tools First
You wire the LLM to real-world capabilities — live web search via Tavily, weather APIs, custom Python functions. The @tool decorator is your best friend here.
② The Brain
An LLM (GPT / Gemini) acts as the reasoning engine. Temperature = 0. No hallucinations. Pure logic.
③ The Prompt — The Most Underrated Part
The ReAct prompt template from LangChain Hub is what tells the model how to think. Most tutorials skip this. Don't.
④ AgentExecutor — The Runtime Engine
This is what runs the thought → action → observation loop automatically. It's the difference between a script and an intelligent system.
⑤ Streamlit UI + Cloud Deployment (Render/AWS)
Ship it. A model no one can access isn't a product — it's a notebook.
What this taught me beyond the tech:
AI Engineering isn't about knowing every framework.
It's about understanding why each layer exists and being able to debug when the loop breaks at 2 AM (it will).

👇
HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embeddings)
Covered so far: chunking, hybrid search, reranking.
Today: HyDE.
What it is:
Given a query, an LLM generates a "fake" hypothetical document that answers it — done around 5 times per query.
Each hypothetical doc gets embedded, and all embeddings are averaged into a single vector.
That averaged vector is used to search the document store instead of the raw query.
The real, similar documents retrieved this way are passed downstream into the generator for the final answer.
Why it's used:
Embedding retrievers often generalize poorly when queries come from domains they weren't trained on.
A short, informal query rarely embeds close to how real documents are actually written on the same topic.
HyDE closes this gap by transforming the query into something that resembles an actual document before searching.
Best used when:
Retrieval recall in your pipeline is weak or inconsistent.
Your queries or documents come from a specialized domain very different from typical retriever training data.
Advantages:
Delivers strong zero-shot retrieval performance without any fine-tuning.
Requires no labeled query-document pairs, which are expensive to collect.
Particularly effective for niche or out-of-domain corpora where standard retrievers struggle.
Disadvantages:
Multiple LLM calls per query add noticeable latency and cost at scale.
If the generated hypothetical documents drift off-topic, retrieval quality can actually get worse instead of better.
What's used instead today:
Most production systems now rely on cross-encoder reranking combined with hybrid search.
Contextual retrieval at the chunking stage is also common — it's cheaper and more consistent than generating fresh documents on every query.
Key insight: HyDE fixes the query-document mismatch at query time, using an extra generation step. Most current pipelines instead fix this mismatch earlier, at the embedding and chunking stage itself.
GitHub: link in comments.
Question for you: have you used HyDE in a live pipeline, or gone straight for reranking instead? Curious what's worked for you.

posts.content:

🧠 Monday Learning: Why Free-Form ReAct Loops Fail in Production (Enter the Plan-and-Execute Pattern) When developers first build autonomous agents, they almost always implement a standard ReAct (Reason + Act) loop. The mechanism feels intuitive: The model receives a goal, thinks about the next step, calls a tool, observes the output, and decides what to do next. It repeats this open-ended cycle until the task is complete. While ReAct works well for simple exploratory tasks, relying on open-ended reasoning loops in high-stakes enterprise pipelines introduces massive architectural instability: Infinite Execution Loops: An agent can get trapped repeating the same failed tool call with micro-variations, burning API credits indefinitely. Context Drift & Goal Amnesia: As tool observations pile up in the context window, the model loses sight of the original objective and wanders off-track. Non-Deterministic Latency: Because the system decides each micro-step sequentially at runtime, you can never predict how long a workflow will take to execute. To build predictable, enterprise-grade agent pipelines, top software architects separate strategic planning from task execution using the Plan-and-Execute Pattern. 🗺️ How the Plan-and-Execute Architecture Works 1️⃣ The Planner: A specialized reasoning model analyzes the overall user request and business constraints. Instead of calling tools directly, it generates a structured, step-by-step directed execution roadmap 2️⃣ The Executors: Individual, lightweight worker agents or deterministic tools execute each planned sub-task in sequence or in parallel. Each executor only receives the specific context and tool required for its individual step, keeping prompt sizes lean and eliminating tool confusion. 3️⃣ The Replanner: After each major milestone or unexpected tool error, a lightweight validator evaluates execution progress against the master plan. If an anomaly occurs, it dynamically updates only the remaining steps rather than restarting the entire workflow from scratch. 🚀 Why This Paradigm Wins in Production Parallel Processing: Independent steps in the generated plan can execute concurrently across multiple workers, slashing overall workflow latency. Predictable Token Budgets: Because the entire workflow isn't stuffed into a single growing context window, token consumption remains linear and predictable. Auditability & Observability: Business stakeholders and operators can inspect the explicit step-by-step roadmap before high-risk mutating tools execute. The Core Realization: Autonomous systems shouldn't figure out the entire journey while they are already driving. Separate the navigation from the engine: plan deterministically first, then execute with precision. Letting AI agents operate in open-ended "reason-and-act" loops is one of the easiest ways to blow up API budgets and trigger infinite execution loops. In production, you have to separate strategic planning from micro-task execution. The Plan-and-Execute pattern creates an explicit, auditable roadmap before a single tool is called. This simple structural shift makes autonomous pipelines faster, parallelizable, and enterprise-ready. Check out today's full breakdown on AI Agent Builder! 👇

The Muse Wonder model will be a key test for Meta’s expensive and rebuilt superintelligence team.
Muse Wonder may mark an important turning point for Meta after a year of enormous investment, aggressive hiring and organisational upheaval.
But reaching the AI frontier is only part of the challenge. The transition from conversational AI to autonomous agents has been slower and more difficult than the industry envisioned.
The commercial opportunity goes far beyond building a better chatbot. It's about creating technology that can reliably accomplish tasks on our behalf, potentially transforming how people interact with Meta's ecosystem and unlocking the value of its enormous AI investments.
I am curious to know if the memory persistence happen natively by the model/API, or does it rely on an external memory store? If Active Memory moves part of memory management from the application layer into the model platform, it could materially change how we design stateful agents.
The real test is whether the rebuilt team can turn research investment into a sustained product advantage. A strong model release can signal progress, but consistent performance in complex workflows, efficient inference costs, and reliable enterprise deployment will determine whether that investment translates into durable business value.
Muse Wonder is designed to carry context across days, recover when work gets difficult, and act across the private systems where a person’s life already sits. Once a model can remember and continue, memory becomes part of the permission structure.
Independent evaluation will settle the frontier claim. Meta’s distribution creates a test no benchmark can reproduce: whether people keep giving the model enough context and authority to finish work that matters. The fuller safety report is still to come.
This isn't a perspective — how can it be a top perspective?

Muse Wonder is designed to carry context across days, recover when work gets difficult, and act across the private systems where a person’s life already sits. Once a model can remember and continue, memory becomes part of the permission structure.
Independent evaluation will settle the frontier claim. Meta’s distribution creates a test no benchmark can reproduce: whether people keep giving the model enough context and authority to finish work that matters. The fuller safety report is still to come.
This isn't a perspective — how can it be a top perspective?

posts.title: Calling AI "superintelligence" won't make it so.
posts.content:
2w
Calling AI "superintelligence" won't make it so. Closing the frontier might. The White House just tried to rebrand AI. It won't stick. No company owns that word. No government owns it. Twitter became X, and the world still says "tweet." Words belong to the people who use them. But the rebrand is the sideshow. Look at why the summit happened. AI safety was becoming the headline: loss of control, runaway models, bills being proposed left and right. The US government needed to show it was ahead of the risk, not behind it. And it needed to show it wasn't going to let China win the race. So it did what governments rarely do well. It got the tech titans in one room, and they showed up. The message was two things: 1. The US will win the AI race against China. 2. The US will define safety on its own terms, with no global rulebook. Read that again. When AI is framed as a race and a national security asset, it stops being open science and becomes a guarded perimeter. Perimeters have gates, and for countries and startups outside them, India's included, the gates get narrower: chips, compute, frontier models, even the rules. Here's what India should learn. The US didn't get here by regulating first and listening later. Government and the people who build the technology were in the same room, aligned on the goal. If we want a seat in this race, our government has to listen to founders and capital as closely as it listens to its own ministries. Otherwise we'll end up in another race we lose. The current government may be great at winning elections. I just wish it were equally great at making India win. (Happy to see a fellow alumni in the pic ;) )

posts.title: Sam Altman's Definition of Superintelligence: AI ...
posts.content:
Sam Altman's definition of superintelligence is the most clarifying thing I've heard on this topic.
Not "smarter than humans in general" — that's too vague to mean anything.
His threshold: AI that can run a major company, lead a top scientific lab, or serve as president better than any human alive.
And the chess analogy cuts deep. There was a window where human + AI beat AI alone. That window closed. The human eventually became the bottleneck, not the advantage.
That's the actual risk model most people aren't tracking. It's not that AI becomes dangerous. It's that human involvement stops being additive — across the exact domains we assumed would always need us.
I usually like your posts. Unfortunately I’m wondering if this one was actually written without you, the human, in the loop? It is profoundly unwise to say that this is a ‘clarifying’ statement by Altman. Chess is a game. Being President of a country of human citizens is one of the greatest human responsibilities there is. Even ‘if’ AGI was better than human + AI, it is clearly not a good idea. Even heads of state still answer to their government structures (let’s say in a democracy). Are they flawed? Yes. Is there corruption, yes as long as time. Are humans ultimately those who have to draw a line where we won’t entertain full AGI, yes. So even if it’s plausible, it’s profoundly unwise. Maybe they could simulate it on Mars first and see how that goes? Also I’d like to hear more from Women in AI on this matter. Please quote Fei Fei Li more. She would never utter such ideas.
Sam’s definition of superintelligence is a category error. Running a company, leading a lab, or being president are institutional roles, not cognitive categories. A system can emulate the outputs of those roles without possessing the cognitive architecture that makes human judgment safe — relational meaning, consequence tracking, invariant detection, coherence stabilization, or moral evaluation.
The chess analogy doesn’t apply. Chess is a closed system with fixed rules and fixed goals. Human cognition is an open system that originates new conceptual universes. AI explores existing spaces. Humans create them. That’s the real distinction — and it’s the civilization‑building capacity Sam’s definition doesn’t measure.
I outlined the underlying cognitive architecture behind this gap here: 🔗 The Discovery of the Human Cognitive Process Steps and the Architecture of Cognition [https://www.linkedin.com/posts/bruce-may\_the-discovery-of-the-human-cognitive-process-steps-activity-7249510975083931648-8k2x](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/bruce-may_the-discovery-of-the-human-cognitive-process-steps-activity-7249510975083931648-8k2x?trk=public_post_comment-text)
The question is, what do we define as better? What are we optimising for?
The chess analogy is interesting, but it exposes a distinction worth examining. Chess has a defined objective and measurable outcomes. Running a company or governing a country involves determining which objectives are legitimate in the first place.
Even if AI becomes demonstrably better at making decisions, superior performance does not independently establish authority to make them. Human participation in execution may become less necessary, but institutional accountability and legitimate authorization remain separate questions.
I think that’s where the more consequential discussion begins.
Right now AI cut so many jobs and investments, that impact on the global economy we start feeling even now. Further will be harder. And we can't handle even that, as humanity.
So how we suppose to benefit from that "or serve as president better than any human alive"?
So, the human who’s “making it worse”, could be the one, who misuses AI and destroys mankind. Is that, what he’s getting at? Maybe, it’s me but the message I keep getting, from the group of seven is “Hey! Don’t blame me if things go wrong. We’ve, done everything we could!”
AI is human data. Without it, it's a pile of nothingness living inside a black hole.
We have become the bottlenecks.
If you endorse it, I know it must be wrong

posts.content:
A few months ago, I mentioned I’m working on a creative project. Today, I’m excited to share what that is: my first book, 📚 Build a Multi-Agent System (From Scratch) for [Manning Publications Co.](https://www.linkedin.com/company/manning-publications-co?trk=public_post-text) The book has officially entered Manning’s Early Access Program (MEAP), meaning you can read the first few chapters today! There’s been a ton of attention on multi-agent systems and the LLM agents that comprise them in recent years. From everyday tasks like web searches to more complex challenges like building entire codebases, LLM agents and multi-agent systems are already being deployed. While by no means perfect, many recognize the potential for agent-to-agent interactions to reshape much of how society functions in the near future. This book takes a hands-on approach to building LLM agents and multi-agent systems from scratch, helping readers gain a deeper understanding of their inner workings. We start by building a single LLM agent from the ground up, implementing the tool-calling process and the task-execution processing loop before progressing towards making our LLM agent MCP-compatible. From here, we’ll incorporate enhancements like memory and human-in-the-loop before assembling multiple LLM agents into a multi-agent system. We’ll explore A2A and other coordination mechanisms to enable multiple LLM agents to collaborate and accomplish tasks. posts.title: Multi-Agent Systems Should Not Be LLM Systems by Default | Louis Liu
posts.content:
𝗔𝗿𝗲 𝘄𝗲 𝗺𝗮𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗰 𝗔𝗜 𝘁𝗼𝗼 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲𝘅? As Multi-Agent Systems grow, we often see: 𝗠𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 → 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗼𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 → 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗟𝗟𝗠 𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘀 → 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗼𝗸𝗲𝗻𝘀 But more complexity does not necessarily mean better outcomes. Every additional LLM call introduces another probabilistic decision. More agent hand-offs can also mean more context loss, latency and opportunities for errors to propagate. So we may end up with: 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲𝘅𝗶𝘁𝘆 ↑ 𝗧𝗼𝗸𝗲𝗻 𝗰𝗼𝘀𝘁 ↑ 𝗟𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗻𝗰𝘆 ↑ 𝗔𝗰𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘆 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗽𝗿𝗲𝗱𝗶𝗰𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆 ↓ This is why I think an 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗯𝗲 𝗮𝗻 𝗟𝗟𝗠. A mature Multi-Agent System should combine LLM agents, deterministic agents, software, ML and humans — using each where it makes sense. And when an LLM repeatedly follows the same reasoning path and calls the same tools, perhaps that logic should be converted into deterministic code. My latest article explores this idea: 𝗠𝘂𝗹𝘁𝗶-𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗦𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺𝘀 𝗦𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗡𝗼𝘁 𝗕𝗲 𝗟𝗟𝗠 𝗦𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺𝘀 𝗯𝘆 𝗗𝗲𝗳𝗮𝘂𝗹𝘁 The next stage of Agentic AI may not be about adding more LLMs. It may be about knowing 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗿𝗲𝗺𝗼𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗺. posts.title: Misusing MAS in LLM research: a call for better integration | Emanuele La Malfa posted on the topic | LinkedIn
posts.content:
🚨 Are we misusing the term Multi-Agent Systems in LLM research? 🚨 Find out more in our latest preprint! As the field of Multi-Agent Systems of Large Language Models (MAS LLMs) rapidly expands, we’re seeing exciting innovations, but also critical gaps. In our latest paper, we argue that many current MAS LLM implementations adopt MAS terminology without grounding in its foundational theory. This can lead to oversimplified architectures and missed opportunities. We highlight four key points: 1. Lack of genuine social agency 2. Poorly designed or absent environments 3. Ad-hoc coordination and communication protocols 4. Shallow or missing metrics for emergent behaviour In other words, MAS has decades of research to offer, yet much of it is being sidelined. We call for: • Clearer terminology • Better integration of established MAS principles • A more rigorous approach to designing truly multi-agent LLM systems Let’s bridge the gap between MAS theory and LLM practice and unlock the full potential of this exciting intersection. Read the article here! 👉 [https://lnkd.in/d5BQ6Bhk](https://www.linkedin.com/redir/redirect?url=https%3A%2F%2Flnkd%2Ein%2Fd5BQ6Bhk&urlhash=P293&trk=public_post-text) A huge thanks to the people who contributed to this work: [Gabriele La Malfa](https://uk.linkedin.com/in/gabrielelamalfa457?trk=public_post-text), [Samuele Marro](https://uk.linkedin.com/in/samuelemarro/en?trk=public_post-text), [Jie Zhang](https://uk.linkedin.com/in/jie-zhang-5326aa187?trk=public_post-text), [Elizabeth Black](https://uk.linkedin.com/in/elizabeth-black-6755ab46?trk=public_post-text), [Michael Luck](https://uk.linkedin.com/in/michael-luck?trk=public_post-text), [Philip Torr](https://uk.linkedin.com/in/philip-torr-freng-frs-1085702?trk=public_post-text) and [Michael Wooldridge](https://uk.linkedin.com/in/michael-wooldridge-1962b2?trk=public_post-text). How Do You Really Evaluate an LLM? If you're deploying Large Language Models, you know that evaluation is the hardest part. [Sebastian Raschka, PhD](https://www.linkedin.com/in/sebastianraschka?trk=public_post-text) 's recent breakdown clarifies the four essential evaluation strategies every ML team should be using: 1. Closed-Form Tests: (e.g., MMLU) – Quick, objective checks for basic knowledge. 2. Programmatic Verification: Using code/logic to check the factual correctness of free-form answers (crucial for grounded QA or code). 3. Human Leaderboards: The gold standard for nuance and safety, but slow and expensive. 4. LLM as a Judge (LLM4Judge): The game-changer for scale. Using a strong LLM to approximate human preference and save on evaluation costs. The takeaway? You can't just rely on one! A robust system uses programmatic checks, starts with objective benchmarks, and strategically uses LLM Judges to scale the crucial human feedback. Really cool open source project by [Ayoola Olafenwa](https://uk.linkedin.com/in/ayoola-olafenwa-003b901a9?trk=public_post-text) , on building multi agent systems that can leverage both web search and agentic RAG to ground LLMs in real world facts.
Super excited to release a new project I’ve been working on: a Multi-Agent RAG Researcher system that can research a topic using both local documents and web search, then generate evidence-based content from it.
I built it with easy-to-follow Python code using the OpenAI API, GPT-5.4, function calling, and tools, with an orchestrator coordinating three worker agents:
✅ Retriever: gathers evidence from local documents and the web using Tavily for web search
✅ Writer: turns that evidence into a grounded draft
✅ Verifier: checks claims before the final answer is returned
I used Qdrant for document retrieval, Tavily for web search, and SQLite for memory, helping the system stay grounded and consistent across the workflow and follow-up questions.
📌 A practical project for anyone interested in exploring RAG, agents, and AI research workflows.

Excited to share my latest project where I designed and implemented a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system from scratch.
Key Highlights:
This project helped me understand how to build scalable AI systems with decision-making workflows, not just chatbots.
Tech Stack: Python, LangChain, LangGraph, ChromaDB, OpenAI
Would love your feedback!
Github link : [https://lnkd.in/dYzWKmGR](https://www.linkedin.com/redir/redirect?url=https%3A%2F%2Flnkd%2Ein%2FdYzWKmGR&urlhash=Nb3F&trk=public_post-text)
Most RAG systems fail in production. Here's why:
Everyone builds: chunk → embed → retrieve → generate.
The problem: basic chunking destroys context. A paragraph about "revenue" split across two chunks loses meaning.
What actually works:
→ Semantic chunking (split on meaning, not character count)
→ Hybrid retrieval (BM25 sparse + FAISS dense vectors)
→ Re-ranking with cross-encoders before sending to LLM
→ Query expansion (generate 3 variants of each user question)
I built this for a knowledge graph + RAG system on Upwork. The jump from naive RAG to this was ~40% improvement in answer quality on the eval set.
The eval framework matters too — RAGAS gives you faithfulness, context precision, and answer relevance. Use it from day 1.

I’ve worked with Python for nearly 10 years. Its biggest achievement is not that it became popular. It became the common interface between disciplines that once operated in completely separate worlds. A single AI project can now touch: → Data processing: NumPy, Pandas, Polars → Machine learning: Scikit-learn, XGBoost, LightGBM → Deep learning: PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX, Keras → Experiment tracking: MLflow, Weights & Biases, Comet → Visualization: Matplotlib, Seaborn, Plotly, Altair → Model serving: FastAPI, BentoML, Gradio, Streamlit → Orchestration: Airflow, Prefect, Kubeflow, Dagster → Data validation: Great Expectations, Evidently, Deepchecks → Privacy and security: Presidio, PySyft → AI agents: LangGraph, LangChain, PydanticAI, CrewAI But the real advantage is not the number of libraries. It is continuity. The same engineer can move from: Raw data → Experiment → Model → API → Agent → Production workflow without switching languages at every boundary. Python is not always the fastest execution engine underneath. Much of the heavy lifting still happens in C++, Rust, CUDA and specialized runtimes. But Python has become the control surface for modern AI. It connects researchers, data engineers, ML engineers, application developers and platform teams through one shared ecosystem. Python did not win because of hype. It won because it consistently shortened the distance between an idea and a working system. If you are building in AI today, Python is no longer just a programming language. It is infrastructure. Which Python library has had the biggest impact on your work?
"Worth adding: this same continuity is also Python's biggest operational risk. When one language touches every layer, a dependency conflict or version mismatch in one library can ripple across the whole pipeline in a way a more siloed stack wouldn't allow."

Python's cross-domain appeal is a double-edged sword. while it fosters collaboration, it also leads to a dilution of expertise. How do you balance broad applicability with the need for deep knowledge in specific areas?

posts.title: One question I keep getting is: Do I need to learn Python to get into AI engineering? In 2015, I started learning R to get into data…
posts.content:

One question I keep getting is: Do I need to learn Python to get into AI engineering? In 2015, I started learning R to get into data science. At the time, R had an amazing ecosystem for statistics, data analysis, visualization, and building explainable data science models. Then Python became more and more popular in data science. Not necessarily because R was wrong, but because Python had a growing ecosystem and was also a general-purpose programming language. I somehow think we are seeing something similar with AI engineering today. AI engineering itself is not language-specific. It is much more system-specific. You can build AI systems in many languages. But right now, a huge part of the AI ecosystem is Python-first: PyTorch, Hugging Face, model training, evaluation, agent frameworks, data tooling, and many of the libraries around them. So, do you need Python to become an AI engineer? Probably not. But does knowing Python make the path much easier because you get access to a much larger AI ecosystem? I think yes. AI engineering is not about Python. But Python is currently one of the easiest ways into the AI engineering ecosystem. What do you think? --- ♻️ Repost to share with others! ➕ We often discuss real-world AI/ML here 👇 ➕ Join 56,000+ AI/ML builders here: [https://lnkd.in/ds_SzEUH](https://www.linkedin.com/redir/redirect?url=https%3A%2F%2Flnkd%2Ein%2Fds_SzEUH&urlhash=SAUy&trk=public_post-text)
Share
yes, and i'd still bet on python for anyone starting today, same way R lost to it: not because the language was better but because the C bindings and tooling investment compounded. PyTorch's ecosystem won on kernel-level work like CUDA graph capture and torch.compile, not syntax. that's the part worth tracking, which layer is getting the engineering investment, not which language reads nicer.
Completely agree. Curious to know what others as well think
Agree on the entry path. Worth adding that the answer changes depending on which part of the system you mean. For training, evaluation and research tooling, Python is the ecosystem and that isn't close. But once a system stops producing output and starts taking action, the constraints change: concurrency, resource bounds, failure semantics, execution boundaries that have to hold under load. Python is unusually good at expressing what should happen and comparatively weak at guaranteeing what cannot. I've built the same stack in both, the execution core in Rust, orchestration and verification in Python and the split wasn't preference. It was where each language stops carrying the guarantee you need. So probably not "which language for AI engineering", but "which language for which layer".
I think the R comparison is what makes this land. You're right, and for the reason you give. One thing I'd add. I'd expect a Python-first stack to make the next hire easier too, since they already know the tools.
Someone coming from JavaScript, Java, Go, or another language shouldn't assume they need to start over. Strong engineering fundamentals still transfer directly into AI systems.
Definitely Python although many years ago I learnt to read and modify R (really, a person developed a script and left the company 😀 ). As whether one needs to know Python - yes, but it's the same as statistics. I cannot write Bellman's formula on a napkin but I know how to do Reinforcement Learning. Also, if someone needs certifications*, I testify that Azure Machine Learning Engineer (AI-300) doesn't require to code but one must read snippets very fast to pass it. * certifications are still needed for consultants or teachers, they do help with credibility when talking to clients or reputation overall; they don't prove any skills though.
The key distinction is between needing Python and benefiting from Python. You can absolutely build AI systems without it, but Python currently removes a lot of friction when exploring models, tooling, evaluation and frameworks.
The distinction between the skill and the ecosystem is important. AI engineering is not inherently Python, but the current tooling makes Python a very useful leverage point.
Learning Python is less about the language itself and more about gaining access to the ecosystem where much of the experimentation and tooling already happens.
The graphic is pretty misleading. Python’s dominance in AI is real, but not because Python itself is inherently faster or because R is somehow “single-threaded.” In both ecosystems, serious numerical workloads often get their speed and parallelism from optimized native libraries underneath, including C/C++, Fortran, BLAS, OpenMP, GPU kernels, and multiprocessing frameworks. Plenty of R packages and workflows are explicitly multithreaded or parallel, while ordinary Python has historically been constrained by the GIL. So presenting Python as “multithreaded” and R as “single-threaded” is using two different definitions of threading. Python’s real advantage is much simpler and much stronger: it has a far larger general-purpose software and AI engineering ecosystem, especially around PyTorch, JAX, deployment, infrastructure, and production tooling. That alone is a compelling reason to learn it. Also, Torch and Tensorflow / Keras have robust R implementations now as well. But claims like “Python is faster, R is slower, Python is multithreaded, R is single-threaded, R has weird syntax” are not serious technical comparisons. They turn a legitimate ecosystem argument into LinkedIn meme science. 😄

**code :**[https://lnkd.in/gM8yAgCE](https://www.linkedin.com/redir/redirect?url=https%3A%2F%2Flnkd%2Ein%2FgM8yAgCE&urlhash=56pe&trk=public_post-text)
(readme file has not added )
As part of building my portfolio, I’ve started developing an **LLM Gateway using FastAPI**, focusing not just on connecting to LLM providers, but also on reliability, security, and production engineering.
Here’s what I’ve implemented so far:
🔹 **Strategy Pattern for Multiple LLM Providers**
Designed the gateway to support multiple providers through a common interface, making it easier to add new providers without changing the core logic.
🔹 **Unified API with SSE Streaming**
Built a single endpoint that streams LLM responses to clients using Server-Sent Events (SSE).
🔹 **Retry Logic with Exponential Backoff and Jitter**
Implemented controlled retries for eligible errors, with exponential backoff and jitter to reduce repeated request bursts and avoid overwhelming providers.
🔹 **Streaming-Aware Error Handling**
Retries are allowed only before the first response chunk is generated. If an error occurs after streaming begins, the gateway sends an error event to the client rather than restarting the stream. Non-retryable errors are returned without unnecessary retries.
🔹 **Structured JSON Logging**
Added structured logs to make requests, failures, and debugging easier to track.
🔹 **JWT Authentication**
Implemented JWT validation to prevent unauthorized clients from accessing the gateway and consuming LLM tokens, helping control unnecessary API costs.
🔹 **Environment-Based Configuration & Git**
Organized configuration using environment variables and environment files, and maintained the project with Git.
🛠️ What’s Next?
My next goals are to strengthen the gateway with:
**Circuit Breaker** — isolate failing providers and prevent repeated unsuccessful calls.
**Observability** — metrics, tracing, and dashboards using Prometheus and Grafana.
**Idempotency** — handle duplicate client requests safely.
**Additional API Endpoints** — expose gateway metrics and available model information.
**Dockerization & Deployment** — containerize the service and deploy it on Render.
**AI-Assisted Self-Healing** — explore intelligent failure analysis and recovery suggestions.
The goal is to build this incrementally, understanding the engineering decisions behind each feature rather than simply integrating tools.
This project is helping me explore the intersection of **backend engineering, distributed systems, and applied AI**, while learning how to make AI services more reliable and production-ready.
Restricting retries to before the first streamed chunk avoids duplicate output and preserves a clean failure contract for clients.
Day 1 of moving from full stack engineering into AI engineering.
I started with the basics of a single LLM API call. A few things changed how I think about building with these models.
Tokens are the real unit. Models read and bill in chunks of about 4 characters, so 1,000 tokens is roughly 750 words. Input and output are priced separately.
The API is stateless. The model remembers nothing between calls, so you resend the whole conversation every turn. Anyone who has built REST services will recognize this. Each request carries everything the server needs and an LLM call is no different.
This is where costs surprised me. A 10-turn chat at 200 tokens per turn is only 2,000 tokens of conversation. Because every call resends the full history you actually send 200 + 400 + ... + 2,000 = 11,000 input tokens.
The context window is a hard limit. Input and output share one token budget per call. Go over it and the call fails. In practice you truncate, summarize or retrieve only what matters.
Temperature and top-p control variety. Temperature 0 picks the most likely token each time, which suits extraction and JSON. Higher values give more varied output. Even at 0 the results are not perfectly deterministic. Top-p limits sampling to the most likely tokens that add up to probability p. Adjust one of them, not both.
Check why the model stopped. A stop sequence ends output on a string you choose. max\_tokens is a hard cap and can cut a response off mid-sentence. I now check stop\_reason before parsing anything. A half-finished JSON object breaks things quietly.
The shape of a call is simple. You send the model name, a system prompt, the messages and sampling settings. You get back content blocks, a stop reason and token usage. Streaming returns the same response as server-sent events so users see text as it arrives.
My main takeaway is that an LLM call behaves like a stateless function. Memory, cost control and validation are the application's job.
For those already building with LLMs, what tripped you up early on?

posts.title: Clean LLM Outputs with Pydantic and FastAPI | Felipe Herrera Arteaga posted on the topic | LinkedIn
posts.content:
Stop writing complex regex to clean up LLM responses in Python! 🛑
When building production-ready AI applications with FastAPI, relying on unstructured string outputs from LLMs is a recipe for broken code and runtime crashes.
The Solution : Pydantic + Structured Outputs
Instead of asking the model for text and hoping it follows your format, enforce strict schema validation at the framework level:
✅ Type Safety: Guarantee that the LLM returns exact data types (integers, lists, booleans, enums).
✅ Native FastAPI Integration: Leverage Pydantic models to automatically map LLM outputs straight into your API responses.
✅ Self-Correction & Retries: Catch parsing errors immediately and send the validation feedback back to the model for automatic retry.
Tip: Treat LLM outputs like untrusted API payloads from an external vendor.
Never bypass validation just because "the prompt asks nicely."
Do you rely on Instructor, LangChain, or native function calling for structured outputs in Python? Let's discuss! 👇
I started treating LLM responses like untrusted third-party APIs, and it completely fixed the random application crashes.
Absolutely! Structured outputs make LLM integrations much more reliable, but schema validation is only one part of the solution. I’d also add retry limits, timeout handling, and semantic validation for business rules. A valid JSON response isn’t necessarily a correct response. Treating LLMs like unreliable external services is the right mindset for production AI systems.
A raw LLM is just a text generator. An AI Harness makes it a reliable software system. 🧠⚡
LLMs aren't software components—they are probabilistic engines. You can't just call an API and hope for the best in production.
That’s where the Harness pattern comes in.
Think of an AI Harness as the scaffolding around your LLM. It manages everything the model shouldn't worry about:
🔹 Tool Orchestration: Safely executing functions (APIs, DB queries, Python code).
🔹 State & Memory Management: Tracking conversation context and persistent memory.
🔹 Guardrails & Fallbacks: Validating structured outputs (via Pydantic) and handling API timeouts or hallucinations.
🔹 Observability & Tracing: Logging prompts, token usage, and step-by-step agent decisions.
The Senior AI Take: Don't spend all your time prompting. Invest in a robust Harness (using FastAPI, Pydantic, and tools like LangChain or custom orchestrators). That's what separates a cool demo from an enterprise-ready AI Agent.
Are you building custom harnesses or relying on out-of-the-box frameworks for your AI workflows? Let’s talk below! 👇
"What exactly is inside an MCP Server?" 🔌
Most of us know that the Model Context Protocol (MCP) is becoming the universal standard (the "USB-C") for connecting AI agents to external systems.
But what actually happens under the hood?
When you build an MCP Server (using Python and FastAPI, for example), you aren't just opening a raw websocket. The protocol standardizes the connection by exposing three core primitives to the AI Client (like Claude, Cursor, or your custom agent):
📂 1. Resources (Read-Only Data)
Think of this as the context layer. The server exposes specific, controlled data to the LLM without allowing modifications. Example: Exposing a live database schema, an internal Confluence wiki page, or system logs via file:// or postgres:// URIs.
📝 2. Prompts (Standardized Instructions)
Instead of hardcoding prompt templates in your client application, the MCP server can serve reusable, parameterized prompt templates. Example: A debug\_error prompt that automatically includes the latest server logs from the Resources layer.
🛠️ 3. Tools (Executable Actions)
This is where the AI takes action. The server exposes strictly typed functions that the LLM can decide to call. Example: An execute\_sql\_query or create\_jira\_ticket function. The execution happens safely on your backend, and the result is returned to the model.
The Architecture:
Your AI orchestrator acts as the MCP Client. It connects to your MCP Server via standard transports (stdio or SSE/HTTP). The model dynamically discovers these Resources, Prompts, and Tools, completely decoupling your enterprise data logic from the LLM routing logic.
Stop writing custom API wrappers for every new LLM. Building a FastMCP server in Python isolates your domain logic securely.
Have you started exposing your enterprise data through MCP yet, or are you still relying on custom LangChain/LlamaIndex integrations? Let’s talk in the comments! 👇
Stop relying on raw text responses from LLMs. It’s time for Structured Outputs in your AI backend. 🚨
A major bottleneck when building production-grade AI microservices is unpredictability. When you ask an LLM for information, it often returns a creative but unstructured text response. For an AI Engineer trying to integrate this response back into a deterministic system (like a database or another API), this is a nightmare.
If your FastAPI application depends on fragile regex parsing or prompt-engineering hacks to extract structured data from an LLM's response:
❌ You increase the risk of run-time failures due to non-standardized outputs.
❌ You introduce unnecessary complexity and latency.
❌ You make your system nearly impossible to validate or test with standard software engineering practices.
The Solution? Pydantic-powered Structured Outputs.
The most efficient way to handle this in Python is leveraging Pydantic models. We don't just ask the LLM for data; we provide it with a strict, strongly-typed contract that defines the exact structure, data types, and constraints of the desired response.
This enables a clean and type-safe integration pattern:
1️⃣ Define the Schema: Create a Pydantic model representing your structured data (e.g., a UserProfile with name, email, and age).
2️⃣ Instruct the LLM: Use tools like LlamaIndex or native LLM features to pass this schema to the model.

🚨𝗬𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗔𝗜 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗺𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗯𝗲 𝘄𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘀𝗮𝗻𝗱𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗼𝗸𝗲𝗻𝘀 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹 𝘁𝗼𝗼𝗹𝘀. 𝗛𝗲𝗿𝗲'𝘀 𝗮 𝘀𝗺𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗮𝗰𝗵.
Most developers focus on choosing a better LLM.
But what if the real bottleneck isn't the model — it's 𝗵𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘀 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝘁𝗼𝗼𝗹𝘀? 👀
I recently came across an interesting approach to MCP tool orchestration called 𝗖𝗼𝗱𝗲 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲. Here's why it caught my attention.
🔹𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺: 𝗧𝗼𝗼𝗹 𝗢𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗵𝗲𝗮𝗱
In traditional tool-calling workflows, an agent may need to discover tool schemas, call tools individually, process intermediate results, and repeat the cycle.
With many tools and large outputs, this can consume valuable context and increase token usage.
🔹𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗜𝗱𝗲𝗮: 𝗖𝗼𝗱𝗲 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲
Instead of making the LLM orchestrate every interaction individually, let it write code that coordinates tool calls.
⚙️ 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗳𝗹𝗼𝘄:
🧠 LLM → Generates Code → Executes Tool Calls → Processes Results → Returns Relevant Output
🔹𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗜𝘀 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴
✅𝗥𝗲𝗱𝘂𝗰𝗲𝗱 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝘅𝘁 𝗯𝗹𝗼𝗮𝘁 — intermediate data can be processed outside the LLM's reasoning context.
✅𝗠𝘂𝗹𝘁𝗶-𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝗲𝘅𝗲𝗰𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 — code can coordinate multiple tool calls in one execution.
✅𝗣𝗼𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝘁𝗼𝗸𝗲𝗻 𝘀𝗮𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀 — the model may need to process only the final, relevant results instead of every intermediate response.
✅𝗕𝗲𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 — separate reasoning from execution instead of sending everything back to the model.
⚠️ One important distinction: Code Mode doesn't automatically guarantee lower token usage. The actual savings depend on the implementation, tool schemas, execution environment, and how much data must return to the model.
Building efficient AI agents isn't just about making models smarter. It's also about reducing unnecessary work around them.
The combination of 𝗠𝗖𝗣 + 𝗖𝗼𝗱𝗲 𝗘𝘅𝗲𝗰𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 + 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝘅𝘁 𝗠𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 is worth understanding if you're building production-grade GenAI applications.
💬𝗤𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗔𝗜 𝗲𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗿𝘀: Would you trust an AI agent to generate and execute code to orchestrate multiple tools, provided it runs in a properly sandboxed environment?

Have you ever wondered how an AI model becomes a real application that people can actually use? 🤔
Training an AI model is just one part of the journey. We also need a way to connect it with websites, mobile apps, databases, and other services. That’s where APIs and FastAPI come in!
💡 𝗛𝗲𝗿𝗲’𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗸𝗻𝗼𝘄:
🔹 𝗙𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗔𝗣𝗜: A Python framework used to build fast and efficient APIs, especially for AI and machine learning applications.
🔹 𝗢𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗔𝗜 𝗔𝗣𝗜: Helps applications access AI models for text generation, image understanding, and more.
🔹 𝗚𝗼𝗼𝗴𝗹𝗲 𝗖𝗹𝗼𝘂𝗱 & 𝗔𝗪𝗦 𝗔𝗣𝗜𝘀: Help integrate cloud-based AI services, storage, and data processing.
🔹 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗔𝗣𝗜𝘀: Allow applications to retrieve, store, and manage data.
🔹 𝗘𝘅𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗔𝗣𝗜𝘀: Connect applications with third-party services such as payment systems, messaging platforms, and weather data.
📌 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝗹-𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗹𝗱 𝗲𝘅𝗮𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲:

posts.title: Optimizing React for High-Frequency AI Streaming | Anees Azhar posted on the topic | LinkedIn
posts.content:
In my recent client project AI stream functioned flawlessly until long messages caused performance problems.
I spent last two days debugging a [Next.js](http://Next.js?trk=public_post-text) AI streaming issue that appeared only with long, complex responses. Short messages worked fine, but longer responses froze the UI for about 10 seconds. The spinner stopped updating, the interface fell behind, and a large chunk of output appeared all at once.
The first implementation used throttled state updates to prevent expensive re-renders, but it failed when the stream became sustained. The problem wasn’t Reacts state batching, it was the synchronization pipeline. I had two different representations of the same data: raw stream output and throttled UI state. As the response grew, the throttled UI state fell further behind the raw stream.
Instead of throttling everything, I changed the architecture
Conceptually :
Raw AI stream > Active message queue > immediate render > Chat history state > throttled updates
or to simplify it
onChunk(chunk) {
renderActiveMessage()
if (!historyUpdateScheduled)
{ scheduleThrottle(() => { updateChatHistory(activeMessageQueue) }) } }
The key change wasn’t removing throttling, but deciding where it belongs. The active UI needs low-latency updates, while the rest of the application doesn’t. This distinction made a bigger difference than optimizing React renders.
My takeway is when dealing with high-frequency streaming data, don’t blindly optimize the stream. Separate the latency-sensitive path from the expensive application-wide state path.
🚀 React DevTools meets AI Agents — A new era of intelligent debugging!
What if your AI coding agent could see your React application the way a developer does?
The React team has introduced "react-devtools-cdt-mcp", an experimental integration that gives AI agents deeper visibility into React applications through Chrome DevTools MCP.
🔥 What makes it exciting?
✅ Component Inspection — Explore the React component tree and identify the components behind UI elements.
✅ Props & Hooks — Inspect component props and hook state to understand application behavior.
✅ Source-Level Debugging — Trace components back to their source locations and owner stacks.
✅ Render Profiling — Analyze component renders, commit timings, and potential performance bottlenecks.
💡 Why does this matter?
AI agents can already inspect the DOM and interact with web pages. Giving them access to React’s component structure and render profiling adds valuable context for debugging complex applications and investigating performance issues.
For frontend engineering teams, this could be another step toward AI-assisted debugging, faster root-cause analysis, and smarter performance optimization.
⚠️ One important caveat: This is experimental and should be enabled only in development builds, as the integration can slow down your application.
🔗 Explore the documentation:
The future of frontend development isn't just AI writing code — it's AI understanding how our applications actually behave.
What possibilities do you see for AI-powered React debugging?
The JS AI story right now isn't which model is smarter. It's who owns the context.
Most teams I talk to still treat agents like a clever autocomplete: open a chat, paste a vague ask, hope the PR looks senior. JetBrains' 2026 numbers say ~90% of pros use agents weekly. That only makes the failure mode louder — you get fluent React that doesn't match your boundaries.
Here's the pattern I keep seeing in reviews:
Don't: a one-liner [AGENTS.md](https://www.linkedin.com/redir/redirect?url=http%3A%2F%2FAGENTS%2Emd&urlhash=jh-H&trk=public_post-text) that says "be a senior React engineer" and "follow best practices". The model already knows that. It will invent a stack, sprinkle "use client", and invent fetch-in-effect patterns you banned two years ago.
Do: treat the context file like an architecture doc the agent can fail against. Pin versions. Name where data lives. List the anti-patterns you actually reject in code review. Force a boundary checklist before it opens a PR.
Why this matters: agent output scales your conventions, or it scales your debt. Vercel's React best-practices skill and the wave of [AGENTS.md](https://www.linkedin.com/redir/redirect?url=http%3A%2F%2FAGENTS%2Emd&urlhash=jh-H&trk=public_post-text) / Cursor rules tooling are the same bet — package framework knowledge so the agent stops guessing.
I'm not arguing for more AI. I'm arguing for less improvisation. If your team can't write the constraints down, the agent can't honor them.
What's in your [AGENTS.md](https://www.linkedin.com/redir/redirect?url=http%3A%2F%2FAGENTS%2Emd&urlhash=jh-H&trk=public_post-text) that an agent could actually violate?
🚀 Built StudyFlow — an AI-powered interactive study tool
Instead of building another AI chatbot, I wanted to explore a different approach:
AI → Structured Data → Validation → Interactive UI
With StudyFlow, users can enter a topic or study notes and generate:
📚 Interactive flashcards

One of the core things I focused on was not trusting raw AI output.
The LLM response is parsed into structured JSON and validated before it reaches the UI. Invalid or malformed responses are handled with proper error states instead of allowing the application to crash.
Tech Stack

🟢 [Node.js](http://Node.js?trk=public_post-text) + Express

The main flow is:
Generate → Parse → Validate → Render → Learn → Retest
I also implemented a three-phase quiz experience where users answer first, reveal the reference answer, see keyword-based evaluation, and then decide whether they know the concept or need to review it.

Day 12 — Learning AI Full Stack 🚀
Diving into LangGraph and learning the different workflow patterns you can build with it — there's a lot more than just "steps in a line."
Sequential — steps run one after another, each depending on the last.
Parallel — multiple steps run at once, then results combine.
Conditional (branching) — the graph decides which path to take next based on the state, like an if/else for agents.
Looping — steps can cycle back and repeat until a condition is met, instead of always moving forward.
Human-in-the-loop — the graph can pause mid-execution and wait for a human to approve or correct something before continuing.
Realizing this is what actually separates a "workflow" from a real agent — the ability to branch, loop, and involve a human, not just execute steps top to bottom. 🚀

Well-done bro 🎉
After nearly a month of late nights, countless iterations, and more coffee than I'd like to admit, I'm excited to introduce the first version of Culinary Velocity. 🚀
This project started from something very personal.
My sister owns a restaurant, and every night after closing, I watched her manually calculate sales, organise bills, and update records. As a software developer, I kept wondering:
"Why is so much valuable time still being spent on repetitive manual work?"
The original idea was simple: build a billing system that automatically records daily sales and exports reports to Excel.
But as I started building, the vision kept growing.
"What if inventory updated automatically?"
"What if payroll could be generated instantly?"
"What if the software could actually help owners make better business decisions?"
That simple billing application evolved into Culinary Velocity.
Today, it's more than a restaurant management system. It's a platform designed to help restaurants operate more efficiently, make smarter decisions, and ultimately increase revenue.
What's included in Version 1?
✅ Kitchen Order Ticket (KOT) with real time order flow
✅ Asset and Inventory Management
✅ Customer Loyalty Programme
✅ Staff and Payroll Management
✅ Financial Reports with Excel export
✅ Online Ordering through a digital menu
My favourite feature: Restaurant Intelligence
Restaurant Intelligence is still in its early stages, but it's already moving beyond traditional reporting.
Instead of simply displaying numbers, it analyses restaurant performance and provides actionable suggestions.
For example, if one branch has a high demand for coffee but limited equipment while another has spare capacity, the system can recommend reallocating a coffee machine to improve service speed and increase revenue.
This is just the beginning. My goal is to build an intelligent operating system that doesn't just manage restaurants but helps owners make better business decisions every day.
Building this first version has taught me far more than writing code. It's been a journey of understanding restaurant operations, solving real problems, and turning ideas into a product that people can use.
There is still a long roadmap ahead, but I'm excited for what's next.
I'd love to hear your thoughts and feedback.
The other day I was walking a client through the web development services I offer.
Halfway in, he stopped me and asked, completely genuinely, no sarcasm in it at all:
"Couldn't I just build all of this myself with Claude?"
Not offended. But he wasn't wrong. The site he was picturing — a few pages, good photos, a contact form .
So I didn't argue. I asked him one question instead.
When someone fills that contact form at 11pm on a Sunday, what happens next?
Long pause.
"It comes to my email. I usually see it the next evening."
And there it is. He never had a website problem.
Here's what I've come to believe: nobody actually needs a website.
A website is a pretty dashboard. It looks good, it makes you feel legitimate, and it does almost nothing. For an early-stage founder that's close to a trap — you spend three weeks agonising over a hero section and launch it feeling like you've built something, when you still have no idea where your leads come from, how many went cold last month, or at which step they stopped replying.
You didn't build a business asset. You built a brochure with a hosting bill.
What actually has value is an operational pipeline.
Something that captures every person who shows interest, no matter which channel they came from. That replies while they're still interested, not the next evening. That follows up on day 2, day 5, day 10 without anyone remembering to. That stops the moment they respond. And that tells you, at the end of the month, exactly where your leads came from, how many converted, and where the rest fell out.
That last part matters more than founders realise. Most early businesses aren't short of enquiries. They're short of any idea what happens to them.
None of that is a website. It's plumbing. It's unglamorous. And AI can't hand it to you finished, because it has to wire into how your business actually runs — not how a business runs in general.
But here's the part I keep thinking about.
That conversation used to need four people. A designer. A developer. A marketer to handle search. Someone to wire up the operations.

Chat-foundry, an open-source npm package for adding AI chat to React, React Native or plain JavaScript apps.
Every time I built an AI chat feature for a client, I rewrote the same logic: message history, streaming responses, loading states, stopping a reply halfway, keeping each user's conversation separate. The UI was always different. The logic never was.
So I turned that logic into a package. chat-foundry handles the chat state and gives you nothing visual, so your app keeps its own design.
What it does:
✅ Works with OpenAI and Anthropic, with real-time streaming
✅ Streaming works in React Native too (no EventSource needed)
✅ Each user gets their own isolated chat session
✅ Pass in user details (name, plan, orders) and the AI uses them in its replies
✅ TypeScript-first, zero dependencies, about 7kb gzipped
The video walks through setup in four steps. 👇
It's MIT licensed and still early (v0.1.5), so I'd really value feedback, issues or a star on

React Native just got faster, here’s why.
For a long time, React Native performance issues were less about JavaScript and more about how the system bridged JS and native code. The new architecture fixes that at the foundation.
Fabric is the new rendering system. It gives React Native a more predictable and synchronous way to update the UI. Layout and rendering are better coordinated, which reduces dropped frames and makes animations feel more responsive, especially in complex screens.
TurboModules replace the old native module system. Instead of loading everything at startup, native modules are initialized only when they are actually needed. This cuts startup time and reduces memory overhead, which is noticeable in real production apps, not just demos.

posts.title: AI Blurs Frontend Backend Lines in Nextjs Project | Honey Sharma posted on the topic | LinkedIn
posts.content:
Once our backend developer interfered with our Nextjs project and it cost the frontend team an hour. Thanks to AI which has blurred the boundary between frontend and backend development. Anyone with a little bit of experience in SDLC and having a powerful AI at hand can build both sides of the software. He was one of our experienced developers. He wrote a simple condition in the code and used NODE\_ENV=prod as an environment variable and prepared the code for production. Soon production welcomed all of us with confusing issues no one from our team had ever seen before. Frontend team started their investigation, running code locally and discussing it with each other. I chose to stay calm and started reviewing commit history patiently. I saw the NODE\_ENV variable used in the code. I knew where the problem was. Next js by default uses the NODE\_ENV variable and sets its values based on the type of script that is running. Standard values that Next js uses for NODE\_ENV: (1). If you run, npm run dev; NODE\_ENV=development (2). If you run, npm run start; NODE\_ENV=production (3). If you run, npm run test; NODE\_ENV=test The official documentation of NextJs recommends against using this variable with custom values. I think in the world of AI accelerated software development it might seem tempting to trust AI too much because of its recently gained capabilities and power but we need to understand that power doesn’t mean you will make the right decision every time. The knowledge of computer science fundamentals will stay relevant for a long time. What do you think?
2,602 followers
One of the biggest mistakes I see in junior developers isn't bad code. It's writing code without understanding the system. I've watched this happen repeatedly. A developer gets a task. They immediately open the IDE. Start coding. Ask for the endpoint. Ask for the payload. Copy the response. Done. But they never ask: Why does this API exist? What is the actual use case? Where does this data come from? What happens after this request? Is there already an API for this? What does the Swagger/API collection say? I've seen frontend developers ask for a direct endpoint when the API collection or Swagger already explains the available contracts. The problem isn't that they don't know an endpoint. The problem is that they don't know the product. And AI is going to make this gap even bigger. If your value as a developer is only: "Give me a ticket and I'll write the code." You're competing with AI at exactly the wrong level. The developers who will stand out are the ones who understand: Product → Use case → System → Architecture → API → Code Not just: Ticket → Code The future developer isn't the person who types the fastest. It's the person who understands what should be built before asking how to build it. That's the skill AI makes more valuable—not less.

The current version includes: 🎙️ Real-time microphone interaction 🎥 Camera integration 🖥️ Screen-sharing support 🧠 Gemini Live API integration 🔊 Real-time AI voice responses 👄 Animated speaking/mouth movement 〰️ Voice visualization 👀 Autonomous eye movement & blinking 😊 Multiple facial expressions 🎭 AI/avatar expression & action architecture 📱 Responsive mobile & desktop UI ⚡ Low-latency real-time interaction The idea is to move beyond the traditional: User → Text → Chatbot → Text and work toward: User → Voice → AI Character → Voice + Expression + Action 🛠️ Tech Stack [Next.js](http://Next.js?trk=public_post-text) TypeScript React Tailwind CSS Framer Motion Google Gemini Live API Web APIs MediaDevices Web Audio API Screen Capture API Vercel GitHub 🧠 Architecture One of the main things I focused on was keeping the avatar system modular. posts.title: Model Context Protocol Enables AI to Connect with External Systems | Femi O. posted on the topic | LinkedIn
posts.content:
Model Context Protocol (MCP): How AI Connects to Real-World Systems Artificial Intelligence has become increasingly capable of understanding language, reasoning, and generating information. But what happens when AI needs to interact with actual business applications, databases, or operational tools? This is where Model Context Protocol (MCP) comes in. What is MCP? MCP is an open standard that enables AI applications to connect with external tools and data sources through a consistent communication interface. Instead of developing separate integrations for every AI application and system, MCP provides a standardized approach to making capabilities available. How does MCP work? MCP involves three main components: 1. MCP Host: The AI application managing the interaction, such as a conversational assistant or coding environment. 2. MCP Client: The component within the host responsible for communicating with an MCP server. 3. MCP Server: A service that exposes selected tools, resources, or capabilities to the AI application. MCP servers can provide Tools for performing operations, Resources for accessing information, and Prompts for reusable workflow templates. A practical example Imagine asking an AI assistant: What is the current status of my support ticket? Without access to the support platform, the AI may not have the information needed to answer accurately. With an MCP integration, the assistant can identify an available ticket-lookup tool, request the information through the MCP client, and receive the result from the MCP server. The assistant can then respond using retrieved information instead of relying on assumptions. Where can MCP be applied? -Customer Service: Accessing CRM records, support tickets, and order information. -Software Engineering: Connecting AI assistants to repositories, issue trackers, and development tools. -Business Automation: Supporting workflows across connected applications. -Data Analytics: Retrieving information from authorized databases and reporting systems. -Knowledge Management: Connecting AI to organizational documents and knowledge repositories. Does MCP replace APIs? No. MCP complements APIs by standardizing how AI applications discover and use external capabilities. MCP servers may communicate with existing systems through their APIs. What about security? MCP is a communication standard, not a complete security framework. Authentication, authorization, access controls, and auditing remain essential. Connectivity should never automatically imply unrestricted authority. The Bigger Picture MCP represents an important step toward interoperable AI systems. Its value is not simply connecting AI to more tools, but enabling meaningful interactions with external systems through standardized interfaces. The future of AI is not just about what models know, but also how effectively and responsibly they interact with the digital world. Every AI tool you've ever used had to be bribed into talking to your other tools. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is changing that. Think of it as the USB-C moment for AI one open standard that lets any AI model talk to any tool or data source the same way, instead of needing a different adapter for every connection. An AI agent built to use MCP can plug into your file storage, your project tools, or your databases without a developer hand-wiring each one individually. This matters more than it sounds like on the surface. It's the difference between AI that works in a single demo and AI that can actually be wired into how your business already operates safely, consistently, and without a new integration project every time you add a tool. This is exactly the kind of foundation we build agentic AI systems on now, because an AI agent is only as useful as what it can actually connect to. If your AI tools still need a custom integration for every new connection, is that a limitation of AI or of how it was built? MCP vs API: Why not use both? APIs connect software to services and data. MCP helps AI applications discover and use tools through a standard interface. Together, they provide a practical foundation for building AI agents. Four principles to remember: Keep authentication, permissions, and business logic in your API. Design MCP tools around tasks, not just individual endpoints. Expose only the tools the agent needs to reduce context usage. Clearly distinguish read operations from write and destructive actions. The key question is not whether to choose MCP or an API. It is how to design the right interface for your AI agent while keeping your existing systems secure and reliable. posts.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP) Beyond Function Calling | Adem Mekonnen posted on the topic | LinkedIn
posts.content:
𝐌𝐂𝐏 𝐢𝐬𝐧’𝐭 𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭 𝐚𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐭𝐨𝐨𝐥𝐬. A common misconception about the Model Context Protocol (MCP) is that it’s simply a standard for function calling. It offers much more than that. MCP defines three foundational primitives: • Actions • Context • Instructions Let’s break them down. 🔹 𝐒𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝟏: 𝐓𝐨𝐨𝐥𝐬 — 𝐓𝐚𝐤𝐞 𝐀𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 Tools expose capabilities an AI model can invoke through an MCP client. 𝐄𝐱𝐚𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐞𝐬: • create\_ticket() • search\_orders() • send\_email() • update\_customer\_record() 𝐓𝐨𝐨𝐥𝐬 𝐞𝐧𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐀𝐈 𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐭𝐨: • Execute operations • Retrieve dynamic results • Interact with external systems 🔹 𝐒𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝟐: 𝐑𝐞𝐬𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐜𝐞𝐬 : 𝐀𝐜𝐜𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐱𝐭 Resources expose data an AI application can retrieve and use as context. 𝐄𝐱𝐚𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐞𝐬: • Documentation and files • Database schemas and records • Project specifications • System configurations 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧: Resources are identified by URIs. They primarily provide information rather than execute actions. Think of them as structured sources of information that an AI application can access when needed. 🔹 𝐒𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝟑: 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐭𝐬 — 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐞 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 Prompts provide reusable templates exposed by an MCP server. They help users initiate structured interactions with an AI model. 𝐄𝐱𝐚𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐞𝐬: • Code review checklists • Incident investigation workflows • Report generation guides • Troubleshooting playbooks Instead of starting from a blank chat, users can select a predefined prompt and supply the necessary inputs. 🔹 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐒𝐢𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐞 𝐌𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐌𝐨𝐝𝐞𝐥: • 𝐓𝐨𝐨𝐥𝐬 → Do things. • 𝐑𝐞𝐬𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐜𝐞𝐬 → Provide context. • 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐭𝐬 → Guide interactions. Understanding these distinctions helps developers design cleaner, more maintainable AI integrations. 🔹 𝐁𝐮𝐭 𝐇𝐞𝐫𝐞’𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐍𝐞𝐱𝐭 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧: 𝐈𝐟 𝐰𝐞 𝐚𝐥𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐲 𝐡𝐚𝐯𝐞 𝐑𝐄𝐒𝐓 𝐀𝐏𝐈𝐬, 𝐰𝐡𝐲 𝐝𝐨 𝐰𝐞 𝐧𝐞𝐞𝐝 𝐌𝐂𝐏? REST APIs enable applications to communicate through defined endpoints. MCP standardizes how AI applications discover and interact with capabilities and context exposed by MCP servers. 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐲 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐞𝐭𝐢𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐬. An MCP server can act as an integration layer over existing systems: • REST APIs • Databases • Microservices This allows AI applications to access selected capabilities through a standardized protocol without requiring you to rebuild your backend. 𝐘𝐨𝐮 𝐧𝐞𝐞𝐝 𝐚 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐝𝐚𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐳𝐞𝐝 𝐰𝐚𝐲 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐀𝐈 𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐭𝐨 𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐭 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐲𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐞𝐱𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐬𝐲𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐦𝐬. The real architectural question isn’t just what your AI can do. 𝐈𝐭’𝐬 𝐡𝐨𝐰 𝐲𝐨𝐮 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐫𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭 𝐭𝐨𝐨𝐥𝐬, 𝐫𝐞𝐥𝐞𝐯𝐚𝐧𝐭 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐱𝐭, 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐫𝐞𝐮𝐬𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐢𝐧𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐬𝐚𝐟𝐞𝐥𝐲 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐞𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐥𝐲. posts.title: 🚀 MCP Explained: The Missing Connection Between AI and the Real World | Avaneesh Yadav
posts.content:
🚀 MCP Explained: The Missing Connection Between AI and the Real World Imagine your AI assistant could securely connect to your databases, search internal documents, interact with GitHub, and use business tools—all through a standard protocol. That’s where Model Context Protocol (MCP) comes in. 👇 🔹 What is MCP? MCP is an open protocol that standardizes how AI applications connect to external tools, data sources, and reusable prompts. 🔹 How does it work? ✅ Host: The AI application you interact with ✅ Client: Manages the connection to an MCP server ✅ Server: Exposes tools, resources, and prompts ✅ JSON-RPC: Structures communication between components 🔹 What can MCP do? 🛠️ Tools — Execute actions, query systems, and call services 📚 Resources — Provide relevant data and context 📝 Prompts — Offer reusable prompt templates and workflows 🔹 Where can you use it? → Connect AI assistants to enterprise knowledge bases → Integrate AI with GitHub and developer tools → Retrieve business data from approved systems → Build AI workflows that interact with external services 🔥 Why does MCP matter? Without a standard protocol, every AI application may need custom integrations for different tools and data sources. MCP provides a common integration layer, helping developers build more reusable and interoperable AI applications. But remember: MCP is not an AI model, and it doesn't automatically make an AI agent intelligent. It standardizes connections; your application still needs the right reasoning, permissions, and safeguards. 🔐 Security is non-negotiable. Before connecting an MCP server: • Apply least-privilege access • Authenticate and authorize remote connections • Validate inputs and tool outputs • Protect credentials and sensitive data • Treat tool responses as untrusted input • Require human approval for high-impact actions 💡 My takeaway: MCP is an important building block for connecting AI applications to real-world systems—but the real value comes from combining it with sound architecture, security, and thoughtful engineering. Want to understand AI, Agentic AI, and software architecture without the unnecessary complexity? posts.title: Model Context Protocol Simplifies AI Integrations | Techsense Developers posted on the topic | LinkedIn
posts.content:
69 followers
If your team is building AI features, you have probably written the same integration more than once: one connector per assistant, per data source, per tool. That cost grows with every new model you try. A recent Contexte Tech article explains why the Model Context Protocol (MCP) is getting attention. It describes MCP as an open protocol that lets an AI assistant call tools exposed by a server, such as search or reading a resource. The same server works with Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, VS Code and any assistant that speaks MCP. According to the article, Anthropic launched it in November 2024 and handed it to the Agentic AI Foundation, part of the Linux Foundation, in December 2025. The article's bigger point: publishers keep their data and expose it through their own server, and answers can carry the source, licence, author and update date. Our view: treat MCP as integration architecture, not a plugin. Before you expose a server, decide who can call which tool, with what credentials, and how every call is logged. Provenance matters too. When we built Nohena, a trade compliance AI, every classification shipped with a rationale, citation and confidence. Takeaway: write the tool once, but design auth and governance before the first call.
Hot take: Your AI agent might not be as intelligent as you think. 👀 What if the real power of AI isn't in the LLM itself, but in the tools you allow it to use? Let's talk about MCP (Model Context Protocol) and tool calling. 👇 Imagine asking an AI: "Find a bug in my code, create a GitHub issue, and notify my team on Slack." A plain LLM can explain how to do these things. But actually performing them requires access to external tools, the right permissions, and a system to execute the actions. That's where things get interesting. 🔹 Tool Calling: The model decides when a tool might help and generates a structured request to call it. 🔹 MCP: Provides a standardized way for AI applications to discover and interact with external tools and resources through compatible MCP servers. 🔹 AI Agents: Can combine reasoning, tool calls, observations, and multiple steps to work toward a goal. But here's the question that keeps me thinking: If an AI agent can call 100 tools, does that make it smarter—or just more capable of making 100 different mistakes? 🤔 More tools mean more possibilities. They can also mean more permissions to manage, more failure points, and a bigger security surface. Maybe the next big breakthrough in AI agents won't be giving them more tools. Maybe it will be teaching them when NOT to use a tool. 💬 Developers, I want your take: 1. Is MCP genuinely changing AI development, or is it primarily standardizing existing integrations? 2. Will MCP become essential for AI agents, or will custom function calling remain enough for most applications? 3. What's more important: better models or better tool orchestration? Let's discuss. 👇 [#MCP](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Fmcp&trk=public_post-text) [#AIAgents](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Faiagents&trk=public_post-text) [#LLM](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Fllm&trk=public_post-text) [#ToolCalling](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Ftoolcalling&trk=public_post-text) [#SoftwareDevelopment](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Fsoftwaredevelopment&trk=public_post-text)

Instead of keeping an AI model isolated, MCP gives it a standardized way to connect with things like databases, APIs, files, and developer tools. For developers building AI-powered applications, this can make integrations much more practical. Definitely something worth exploring.
