Looking back, Spring AI didn't just teach me a new framework—it helped transform my profile from a Java Microservices Developer into an AI Developer. The journey has just begun, and I'm excited to keep exploring agentic AI, RAG architectures, MCP, and enterprise AI solutions. This approach allows developers to bridge the gap between static language models and dynamic, real-world APIs. 𝗛𝗶𝗴𝗵𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁𝘀 & 𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗧𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗮𝘄𝗮𝘆𝘀 • Use DTOs to explicitly define request parameters and API response structures. • Implement the Function interface from Java's utility library to wrap service logic. • Register custom functions as Spring Beans with descriptive metadata for the LLM. • Leverage OpenAIChatOptions to register functions within the chat model context. • The LLM intelligently parses user queries to decide if an external function call is necessary. • Use URIComponentsBuilder to safely and cleanly construct external API requests. By leveraging function calling, applications can provide up-to-date, accurate answers that require external lookups, significantly increasing the utility of LLM-based services. 👉 Watch the full video to dive deeper into the implementation. TechyTacos demonstrates how to refine RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) in Spring AI to ensure LLM responses are derived strictly from specific text files rather than generic training data. 𝗛𝗶𝗴𝗵𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁𝘀 & 𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗧𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗮𝘄𝗮𝘆𝘀 • Utilize a system prompt to provide explicit instructions and constrain the LLM's scope. • Store custom instructions in a dedicated file with the .st suffix to maintain a clean template structure. • Use SystemPromptTemplate to dynamically map document content to the prompt variable. • Convert similarity search results from a list of documents into a single string for context injection. • Implement user and system messages separately to structure the chat interaction effectively. • Pass a list of messages to the prompt object to maintain a clear separation between the query and the context. • Return responses in JSON format for better integration with downstream applications. By routing queries through structured context injection, you eliminate generic hallucinations and ensure high-accuracy, document-specific output. 👉 Watch the full video to dive deeper into the implementation. posts.title: Things Every Engineer Should Know: AI Agents A simple way to think about an AI agent is as a while-loop. But there’s a lot happening…
posts.content:
Things Every Engineer Should Know: AI Agents A simple way to think about an AI agent is as a while-loop. But there’s a lot happening inside each iteration. At the center is the 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹. Think of it as the brain of the agent. It reasons over the available context and decides what should happen next. 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝘅𝘁, 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗲, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗠𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆 give the model the information it needs. Context is what it can see right now. State tracks what has happened during the task. Memory preserves useful information that can be retrieved later. 𝗧𝗼𝗼𝗹𝘀 give the agent hands. The model can decide what needs to happen, but tools let it actually do something about it. They're functions the model can call to query a database, call an API, execute code, search the web, or work with files. The 𝗛𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀 is the system around the model that coordinates everything. It assembles context, calls the model, executes tools, feeds the results back in, updates state, and controls the execution loop. Together, these pieces create the 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗟𝗼𝗼𝗽: Context → Reason → Act → Observe → Update → Repeat Each iteration gives the agent new information to reason over, allowing it to adapt what happens next instead of trying to solve the entire task in a single model call. But not every agent loop is equally sophisticated. A basic loop might just connect an LLM to tools. Add memory and lifecycle management, then more deliberate context and harness engineering, and each level introduces new capabilities and complexity. Oracle provides a great breakdown of this progression through 𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗲 𝗹𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹𝘀 engineers should understand. posts.title: AI Agents Think and Adapt Through Iterative Loops
posts.content:
6 followers
𝗛𝗢𝗪 𝗗𝗢𝗘𝗦 𝗔𝗡 𝗔𝗜 𝗔𝗚𝗘𝗡𝗧 𝗔𝗖𝗧𝗨𝗔𝗟𝗟𝗬 𝗧𝗛𝗜𝗡𝗞? 🧠🤖
AI agents don’t simply generate one response and stop.
An agentic system can work through an iterative loop:
𝗚𝗼𝗮𝗹 → 𝗢𝗯𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗲 → 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝘀𝗼𝗻 → 𝗣𝗹𝗮𝗻 → 𝗔𝗰𝘁 → 𝗖𝗵𝗲𝗰𝗸 𝗥𝗲𝘀𝘂𝗹𝘁 → 𝗥𝗲𝗽𝗲𝗮𝘁
The agent evaluates the current situation, decides what needs to happen next, uses available tools, observes the outcome, and adapts its next action.
That loop is what makes agentic systems useful for multi-step tasks rather than simple question-answering.
The key idea: an AI agent is not just generating an answer - it is working toward an objective.
🤖 \*\*What is Agentic AI?\*\*
AI is moving beyond simply answering questions.
\*\*Agentic AI\*\* refers to systems that can understand a goal, reason about what needs to be done, create a plan, use tools, observe results, and adapt their actions to complete the task.
A simple way to understand an AI Agent:
\*\*Perceive → Reason → Plan → Act → Observe → Adapt\*\*
For example, instead of only answering \*“Which restaurants are nearby?”\*, an AI agent can search for restaurants, check ratings, filter the results, and present the most relevant options.
The key building blocks are:
🧠 LLM
💾 Memory
🛠️ Tools
📋 Planning
⚡ Actions
\*\*LLM + Memory + Tools + Reasoning + Actions = AI Agent\*\*
This is just the foundation of Agentic AI. There’s much more to explore — from tool calling and RAG to workflows, LangGraph, and multi-agent systems.
What concept should I cover next?
AI can produce an answer in seconds. The challenge is knowing whether it is the right answer. I use AI to explore ideas, improve a first draft and understand unfamiliar subjects more quickly. It can remove some repetitive work and help turn a blank page into a useful starting point. But speed can create a new problem: when something looks polished, it is easy to assume it must also be correct. AI can sound very confident.
Unfortunately, confidence is not a unit test.The real productivity gain does not come from accepting everything AI produces. It comes from combining its speed with our own experience, judgement and responsibility.

What is an AI agent? And how does it differ from traditional LLMs?
I created this friendly visual to highlight what constitutes what an AI agent is.
AI agents are AI systems that can take a goal, determine what steps are needed, use tools or software to act, evaluate the results, and continue working until the task is complete.
The key difference from a traditional LLM is that an LLM primarily generates a response, while an AI agent can use that intelligence to take actions and work toward an objective.
Think of an AI agent like a junior employee: instead of giving them every individual step, you give them an objective, they figure out what needs to be done, use the tools available to them, check their work, and continue until the assignment is complete.
AI can give you thousands of answers.
But the decision is still yours.
We are entering a world where AI can write, analyse, predict, create and recommend faster than ever.
But there is one thing AI should never replace — human judgement.
The real AI skill is not knowing how to get more answers from AI.
It is knowing:
AI should make us more capable, not more dependent.
Use AI as your assistant.
Not as your decision-maker.
Think. Verify. Decide.
71 followers
The conversation around AI often starts with fear: Will AI replace my job?
Perhaps there is a more useful question: How can AI make me better at what I already do?
The professionals who thrive in the next decade may not necessarily be the best programmers or AI experts. They may be the people who learn how to combine technology with judgment, creativity, communication, and deep domain expertise.
AI is changing the tools. It doesn't eliminate the need to think.
What is one part of your work that AI has already changed?

posts.title: What are Agentic Loops in AI Agents | Carles Vallecillo posted on the topic | LinkedIn
posts.content:
Loop… James Loop Agentic Loops are a buzzword in the IT industry right now and rightfully so. What are they? Why should you care? Let’s cover this and more: If you’re familiar with programming, you’re probably very familiar with loops. Well, it is the same idea applied to an AI Agent. Now, when does the loop end? Easy -> when the task is achieved. Say you are trying to get a cheap flight to NZ. First iteration of the loop, the flight is booked, all is sorted? Great. Job done ✅ The most likely reality, however, is that this will take a few iterations. So in essence, an Agentic Loop is nothing but a natural process that an AI Agent goes through (did I say natural and AI in the same sentence?? Sorry!!! 😨). In other words, agentic loops are the ‘while’ loops that an Agent will create itself while trying to achieve your task. Back to the example of a NZ flight, imagine the Agent notices that flights on Thursdays are $300 cheaper. Then it may check if you are open to trying different airports. Then circle back and pick an option. If you say No, it adjusts again. And so on. Unlike a common program: the path isn’t set beforehand (A -> B -> C). It varies, and the agent decides its next steps – always according to your instructions of course (see my previous article on AI Harness: [https://lnkd.in/gtdBWMwf](https://www.linkedin.com/redir/redirect?url=https%3A%2F%2Flnkd%2Ein%2FgtdBWMwf&urlhash=O7cc&trk=public_post-text)). And a subtle note there: this behaviour is precisely what makes it ‘agentic’ rather than classic automation. Classic automation can branch too – but every branch was pre-written by a human in advance. An agentic loop decides its next step at runtime, based on the situation in front of it, including situations that nobody explicitly coded for. The structure can vary, but it usually follows this pattern: while (goal not achieved) { 1. Assess – what is the current situation? 2. Decide – what will the next step be }   Like in the old days of infinite recursive Lambda calls (limits? Who needs those), now we can get infinite Agent loops – and that is why I cannot afford to buy more RAM to play DooM anymore 🔫 As an example, you can see the one I used for the AI Agent that calls my Food MCP server: [https://lnkd.in/gVC8EaSb](https://www.linkedin.com/redir/redirect?url=https%3A%2F%2Flnkd%2Ein%2FgVC8EaSb&urlhash=eNZ6&trk=public_post-text) It pretty much follows this loop: First reads a request and then -> while (not able to answer request yet) { 1. Assess – what is the current situation? 2. Decide which tool to call next } And finally answer the request Pretty simple in concept - with code it just gets a bit longer. Excellent point - reliable agentic systems need explicit stop conditions, iteration budgets, and observability, not just better reasoning. Question: Which signal is most useful for detecting a runaway agent: iteration count, cost, or repeated actions?
Excellent breakdown. 👏 Agent loops are easy to prototype but much harder to make reliable in production. Clear termination rules, iteration budgets, and no-progress detection are essential to prevent agents from becoming unpredictable or unnecessarily expensive. The focus on observability is especially valuable. 🚀
Stop rules and budgets are necessary, but the ugly failure is replay. If a loop retries after a timeout, the tool call may have succeeded while the agent thinks it failed. posts.title: AI Systems Require Iteration and Feedback Loops
posts.content:
The more AI events I attend, the more one pattern keeps showing up:
The first version of an AI system is rarely the finished system. The iteration loop is where the real engineering happens.
I saw this again at the Snowflake event yesterday while discussing semantic context.
The idea was simple:
USE → TUNE → LEARN → REPEAT 🔁
Users interact with the system.
We observe where retrieval fails, where the model misunderstands business terminology, where an agent chooses the wrong tool, or where the output simply doesn’t match what the user expected.
Then we tune.
Prompts.
Semantic definitions.
Retrieval and reranking.
Context.
Tools.
Evaluation.
Guardrails.
Then users interact with it again — giving us another set of signals to learn from.
What stood out to me is that this isn’t really a Snowflake-specific concept.
I’ve seen the same pattern repeatedly across AI systems, RAG pipelines, agents, evaluations, and production ML.
You don’t just build → deploy → finish.
You:
Build → Evaluate → Observe → Learn → Improve → Repeat. 🔁
And as AI systems become more agentic, I think this feedback loop becomes even more important.
A model may be powerful.
But a system that continuously learns where it fails and gives engineers a way to improve it is what becomes useful in production.
That was one of my biggest takeaways from today’s sessions.
AI engineering is increasingly becoming iteration engineering.
AI Engineer's Production Notes #009 - GraphRAG
Vector search finds text that sounds similar. It doesn't know that two facts are actually connected.
GraphRAG fixes that by turning your knowledge into entities and relationships first - then retrieving through those connections, not just embedding distance.
The 6 pieces that make GraphRAG work:
Watch for: duplicate entities that never got merged, noisy relationships from low-quality extraction, communities so large their summaries turn vague, and a graph nobody scheduled to update — none of these look broken until a multi-hop question comes back wrong.
Simple rule: build the graph for connections, keep vectors for semantic detail, and only take on GraphRAG when your questions genuinely need multi-hop reasoning or whole-dataset answers.
➕ Follow [Shubham Gadade](https://in.linkedin.com/in/shubham-gadade-396a521a4?trk=public_post-text) for more on AI agents, LLMs, and production ML.
📕 Save this if you're building RAG systems.
Repost for someone whose vector search keeps missing the obvious connection.
Is it Machine Learning or GenAI? The Modern Business Scientist’s Dilemma 📊🤖
For a long time, data science was all about traditional ML—building predictive models on structured data to drive precision, optimization, and hard ROI.
Today, Generative AI has completely transformed the playbook. We are moving from strict numerical forecasting to cognitive automation, RAG systems, and agentic workflows that process unstructured human data at scale.
But here is what I’ve learned: It’s never an "either/or" choice.
👉 Traditional ML gives businesses the precision to optimize what is happening.
👉 GenAI gives businesses the agility to synthesize why it matters and scale unstructured workflows.
The true power of a Business Scientist lies at this intersection—combining quantitative rigor with cognitive intelligence to build enterprise solutions that actually move the needle.
How is your team balancing traditional predictive models with GenAI initiatives? Let’s discuss in the comments! 👇
**I stopped asking one powerful model to do everything.**
That sounds obvious, but it’s an easy trap in production AI.
If one model is doing reasoning, classification, comparison, explanation, formatting, routing, and validation, you may be paying for capability where you don’t actually need it.
A better pattern is to allocate intelligence by task complexity:
**High ambiguity / deep reasoning** → capable model
**Narrow semantic explanation** → smaller fast model
**Exact output shape** → typed schema / validation
**Predictable control flow** → deterministic code
The important shift for me was this:
**Don’t ask a model to solve something code already knows.**
If software can detect a mismatch deterministically, let software detect it.
Then use a smaller model only for the part that is actually semantic: explaining that mismatch clearly.
This same idea shows up in real systems like document extraction, support triage, RAG review, and content pipelines.
It also reminded me of TypeSafe’s Jev, which explores structured decision-making through typed questions and outputs rather than relying entirely on free-form text generation.
Reference: [https://lnkd.in/gbJbjVPt](https://www.linkedin.com/redir/redirect?url=https%3A%2F%2Flnkd%2Ein%2FgbJbjVPt&urlhash=wOAa&trk=public_post-text)
**The goal isn’t to use smaller models everywhere.**
**It’s to use the smallest amount of intelligence necessary for each step.**
In AI, knowing how to build a model is not enough.
One thing that can truly set you apart is understanding the context behind what you're building.
You can have a model with impressive accuracy.
You can explain the algorithm.
You can discuss the architecture, parameters, and metrics.
But can you explain:
Why was this problem worth solving?
What does this prediction actually mean for the business?
What could happen if the model is wrong?
Why did the model make this particular decision?
And can you explain all of that to someone who doesn't know anything about machine learning?
If you can't, you may understand the technical side of the model without fully understanding the problem you're solving.
This is why human context matters.
AI doesn't operate in isolation.
Models are built for people, businesses, and decisions that exist in the real world.
The goal isn't just to build a model that works.
It's to understand what it is doing, why it matters, where it can fail, and what its output means in the real world.
Technical knowledge builds the model.
Context helps you build the right solution.

posts.title: AI Agent Executes End-to-End Research Run on Top-Tier ...
posts.content:
What actually happens when an AI agent is given an accepted top-tier conference paper and tasked with pushing beyond it?
Following our announcement of **ScientistTwo**, here is a look at the system executing an end-to-end research run on our platform.
The core issue with automated scientific discovery isn't generating plausible prose—it's empirical verifiability. If an agent cannot isolate causal mechanisms, test its code across diverse datasets, and survive peer review, it's just curve-fitting.
Across our benchmark of 107 problems from ICLR, ICML, and NeurIPS, here is how ScientistTwo navigates the scientific lifecycle without human guidance:
**- Limitation Extraction & Novelty Search:** It analyzes the input paper (e.g., Mind-the-Glitch), isolates theoretical bottlenecks, and scores candidate ideas for novelty before committing compute.
**- Subset-First Screening:** Reproduces baselines on benchmark slices first to discard unpromising directions quickly and protect compute budgets.
**- Ablation-Driven Pruning:** When an idea shows signal, it executes systematic component ablations, actively pruning mechanisms that fail to contribute to performance gains.
**- Active Rebuttal Engine:** During simulated peer review, the Rebuttal Agent writes code and runs supplementary experiments to defend the paper with empirical evidence rather than mere editorial edits.
**- Chain-of-Evidence Audits:** Every accepted artifact undergoes strict automated audits—0 of 1,814 references hallucinated, zero specification violations/reward hacking, and verified method-to-code alignment.
**- Interactive Butler:** Through the Polaris Butler sidecar, researchers can inspect the full decision graph, reviewing why intermediate ideas were rejected or modified.
You can read all 86 autonomously generated manuscripts spanning 8 fields—from LLMs and robotics to neuroscience and optimization—in our interactive paper gallery.
Explore the platform run trajectories, codebases, and generated papers:
🌐 Project: [https://lnkd.in/gJsTPDje](https://www.linkedin.com/redir/redirect?url=https%3A%2F%2Flnkd%2Ein%2FgJsTPDje&urlhash=h8sU&trk=public_post-text)
📄 Paper: [https://lnkd.in/gXjiGpDE](https://www.linkedin.com/redir/redirect?url=https%3A%2F%2Flnkd%2Ein%2FgXjiGpDE&urlhash=EuPz&trk=public_post-text)
The experiment-driven rebuttal loop is especially interesting. In our research workflow, we’ve been focusing on the reverse transition too: when a supplementary experiment undermines the central claim, can the system narrow or withdraw it and revisit dependent conclusions? Do your trajectories include examples of that? Those would be valuable complements to the successful manuscripts.
What stood out to me is the emphasis on checking the work, not just generating it.
In science, getting an answer quickly is helpful, but understanding why it holds up across different conditions is what lets others build on it later.
I love the idea of being able to trace why certain directions were dropped along the way. That kind of transparency makes autonomous research feel much more trustworthy.
Subset-first screening controls cost well. The key check is whether early pruning ever drops ideas that only separate at full scale.
The subset-first screening is the piece I'd audit hardest. It saves compute, but it can also reward ideas that fit an unrepresentative slice and kill mechanisms whose gain appears only at full scale. Reporting how often early ranking flips on the full benchmark would make the 80.4% success rate much easier to interpret.
Two immediate questions come to mind: 1- what does "without human guidance" exactly mean? are we talkig completely autonomous? 2-how robust is the result if you run it on the same paper more than once?
Very cool. We are very similar. We also let our AI agents evaluate current research papers and validate that analysis using in house tools. Since the tool runs are all deterministic, we also included heartbeat provenance trails that made sure that there was no hallucinations along the way.
Software used to be part of the moat in computational chemistry. Increasingly, it isn’t.
Dave captures the implication perfectly:
“The tools are getting cheap. The judgment needed to use them well isn’t.”
AI can dramatically compress the distance between “I wonder if…” and a working computational tool. But it does not eliminate applicability domains, validation, experimental evidence, or the scientific judgment required to know whether an answer is meaningful.
As implementation becomes easier, the moat moves upstream: better questions, better models, better data, and better scientific judgment.
When everyone can build the tool, what becomes scarce?
Refine the LinkedIn post
Every paper today claims to be "State-of-the-Art."
Yet when you sit down to reproduce the benchmarks:
❌ The repository is missing or incomplete.
❌ The performance collapses in practical settings.
❌ The results rely on undocumented hyperparameter tuning or ungodly amounts of compute.
AI research was intended to push boundaries and solve meaningful problems. Somewhere along the line, it turned into a race for social media clout and marketing announcements.
When every publication claims to be "groundbreaking," genuine innovation gets drowned out. We’ve traded rigorous validation for absolute metrics and PR-ready headlines.
If independent researchers, students, and smaller labs can't verify or replicate findings, is it truly scientific progress—or just corporate theater?
Real progress isn’t measured by how loud a preprint sounds on social media; it’s measured by whether it holds up when tested outside the lab that built it.
What’s been your experience trying to replicate recent "SOTA" papers?
AI can summarize a 30-page research paper in 10 seconds.

Can quantum computing actually make machine learning better? The interesting answer isn't simply yes or no. Quantum Machine Learning (QML)explores whether quantum computing methods can provide meaningful advantages for specific machine-learning tasks — from kernel methods and dimensionality reduction to parameterized quantum circuits and optimization. But there is an important distinction that often gets lost: Theoretical speedup ≠ simulator result ≠ practical advantage on real hardware. In our latest Research article, we examine QML through a more specific question: Under what conditions can quantum-computing methods offer a meaningful advantage for machine-learning tasks — and what evidence would actually establish it? Three points stand out: → Advantage claims need a defined task, representation and hardware environment. →Noise, decoherence and data-loading costs remain major constraints for near-term applications. → The meaningful comparison is not “quantum vs classical” in the abstract, but hybrid quantum-classical workflows vs strong classical baselines on the same defined problem. Quantum Machine Learning remains a fascinating research frontier. But theoretical potential should not be confused with demonstrated production advantage. posts.title: Quantum Advantage Timeline Updated: Machine Learning, Chemistry, and Cryptography | Marin Ivezic posted on the topic | LinkedIn
posts.content:
I keep track of when each industry can expect a quantum advantage, and I have just updated that work, a seven-part series. I collect the published resource estimates for fault-tolerant algorithms and map each one to the business problem it would solve. Then I compare those requirements with hardware progress, from vendor roadmaps to demonstrated results, to estimate when a machine large enough will exist. The largest change over the last few months is in quantum machine learning. In April, Zhao, Preskill, Huang and four co-authors proved an unconditional exponential quantum advantage in memory for classification and dimension reduction on streamed classical data. Because the result is unconditional, no classical algorithm can match it in memory. Machine learning still has no hardware timeline, though, because nobody has published what executing that advantage would cost at commercial scale. The second is cryptanalysis. The narrowest published circuit for 256-bit elliptic-curve cryptography needs 835 logical qubits, at 24 to 34 times the Toffoli gates of the Google and Schrottenloher circuits. RSA-2048 needs roughly 1,400 logical qubits. Most grand-challenge chemistry needs as many logical qubits or more, so a cryptographically relevant quantum computer may arrive alongside the chemistry that justifies these machines, or before it. A new paper I’ve been working on is now available in ACM Transactions on Quantum Computing. The starting point is simple: not all qubit readout measurements are equally reliable. Yet many classification methods, including machine learning approaches, immediately turn the signal into a binary decision, discarding useful information about uncertainty. In this paper, we introduce an approach based on Fuzzy C-means clustering and data filtering. Instead of treating every measurement in the same way, the method assigns a confidence level to each outcome and selects the most reliable shots. We tested it on four real IBM quantum devices, from single- and two-qubit readout to the reconstruction of GHZ and W states with up to 10 qubits. The results show a 2–3% improvement in assignment fidelity, with statistically significant gains in more than 94% of the GHZ experiments and 97% of the W-state experiments. posts.title: Quantum error correction — the genuinely hard engineering problem standing between today's noisy, error-prone quantum hardware and a…
posts.content:
3w
Quantum error correction — the genuinely hard engineering problem standing between today's noisy, error-prone quantum hardware and a fault-tolerant quantum computer capable of practically useful computation — has become one of the more interesting, underappreciated applications of machine learning in 2026. Why this specific application makes genuine sense as a strong current fit for AI: identifying and correcting quantum errors in real time requires pattern recognition across enormously complex, high-dimensional quantum state information, faster than a human or a traditional deterministic algorithm could realistically process — exactly the kind of pattern-recognition-at-scale problem machine learning excels at. What progress on this front actually unlocks if it continues to advance: faster, more effective error correction directly translates into quantum computers that can run meaningfully longer and more complex calculations before accumulated errors overwhelm the result — potentially the single most important practical lever for reaching genuinely useful, fault-tolerant quantum computing sooner than current hardware roadmaps alone would suggest. Why this matters even if you have no plans to work in quantum computing yourself: it's a clear, concrete example of a broader, genuinely important pattern — using today's mature AI capability to accelerate progress in adjacent deep-tech fields, rather than AI and other emerging technologies developing in complete isolation from each other. The AI-quantum intersection worth actually paying attention to in 2026 isn't the speculative "quantum AI supercomputer" narrative. It's this quieter, more concrete story of AI genuinely helping build better quantum hardware today. This shift rewards architects who think in systems and trade-offs, not just engineers chasing the newest tool of the month. -Ravi Kumar Gupta [#QuantumComputing](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Fquantumcomputing&trk=public_post-text)[#MachineLearning](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Fmachinelearning&trk=public_post-text)[#AIresearch](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Fairesearch&trk=public_post-text)[#DeepTech](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Fdeeptech&trk=public_post-text)[#EmergingTech](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Femergingtech&trk=public_post-text)[#Innovation](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Finnovation&trk=public_post-text)
Share
One additional challenge is that quantum error correction is not only a pattern-recognition problem. It is also a real-time control problem under hardware drift. A decoder may perform extremely well on the error distribution it was trained on and still degrade if noise characteristics change, calibration shifts, crosstalk evolves or the device enters a regime that was poorly represented in training. So the strongest AI contribution may not be simply “better decoding”, but adaptive decoding: systems that can detect when the noise model has changed, update safely and still meet the latency constraints required for fault-tolerant operation. In that sense, the hard problem is not only learning the error patterns. It is knowing when the patterns themselves have changed.

What If I Told You One Company Makes Machines That Are Critical to Building Some of the World’s Most Powerful Chips? 🤯
1: Meet ASML 🇳🇱 — a company from the Netherlands that makes some of the most advanced lithography machines in the world. These machines help chip manufacturers print incredibly tiny patterns onto silicon wafers, which is a key step in making modern semiconductor chips.
2: And here’s where it gets interesting… ASML’s EUV machines use extremely short-wavelength light to create some of the smallest features needed for advanced chips. These machines are incredibly complex, contain thousands of components, and can cost hundreds of millions of dollars.
3: But where does NVIDIA come in? NVIDIA designs powerful AI chips, but it doesn’t manufacture most of them itself. Companies like TSMC manufacture many of NVIDIA’s advanced chips, and TSMC uses ASML’s lithography technology in its chip factories.
4: So the connection is simple: ASML → lithography machines → TSMC → NVIDIA chips → AI systems. 🤯
That’s why ASML is considered one of the most important companies in the global semiconductor industry. Its machines are helping enable the chips powering AI, smartphones, cars, data centers and much more.
What do you think about ASML’s technology? Comment below! 👇

NVIDIA-BACKED BEAM ANNOUNCED: ARE WE ENTERING “AI CHIP/MODEL MADNESS”? E=MC² | October 6, 2026 SCORECARD TIME! NVIDIA is in the AI model business. OpenAI is moving into silicon. Elon Musk’s companies are pursuing Terafab to secure their own chips. Where do these “industries” begin and end? The boundaries are dissolving. A customer becomes a competitor. A supplier becomes an investor. A model developer becomes a chip designer. Each wants more control over the economics of intelligence. THE SCORECARD 1. NVIDIA → MODELS Reflection AI, backed by NVIDIA, announced Beam on October 5. Reflection develops Beam; it is not an NVIDIA-owned model. NVIDIA also has its own Nemotron model family. Beam has 501 billion total parameters, with 23 billion active per token. Reflection claims reasoning performance comparable to GLM-5.2 using 3–4 times less inference compute. Independent validation remains essential. 2. OPENAI → SILICON OpenAI and Broadcom have announced a 10 GW custom-accelerator collaboration. OpenAI designs the accelerators and systems with Broadcom. That makes OpenAI a hardware architect as well as a model developer; it does not make it a semiconductor foundry. 3. MUSK’S ECOSYSTEM → CHIP PRODUCTION Terafab is a planned semiconductor manufacturing initiative involving Tesla, SpaceX and xAI, with Intel support. Its ambition connects captive chip demand with AI, vehicles, robotics and space infrastructure. A manufacturing plan must still become qualified, economical production. WHY CROSS THE BOUNDARIES? Model companies want lower inference costs, reliable capacity and hardware tailored to their workloads. Chip companies want software ecosystems that encourage adoption of their hardware. Integrated operators want control over chips, models, power, distribution and the customer relationship. My view: the contest is shifting toward who can turn the whole system into durable cash flow. BUT INTEGRATION HAS A PRICE • Capital commitments grow across multiple businesses. • Partners can become rivals while remaining indispensable suppliers. • Rapid model improvements can change hardware requirements. • Long-lived factories and power assets must serve fast-changing technology. • Announced capacity can outrun profitable customer demand. For E=MC², this is scorecard territory: useful output per watt, cost per completed task, utilization, capital recovery and asset-tenor mismatch. A benchmark victory does not establish a profitable business. A chip design does not establish manufacturing yield. A gigawatt commitment does not establish return on capital. Are we entering AI chip/model madness? Possibly. We are certainly entering a period when familiar industry labels reveal less about what a company actually does—and where its risks sit. Follow the money, the dependencies and the payback. 🇺🇸 Excellent FT piece on how AI is transforming debt markets. Investors have lent roughly $500B to AI-linked borrowers this year. The hyperscalers alone are expected to issue over $1T more in the next few years. I genuinely wonder, though, why lenders would agree to deploy that much capital into centralized AI infrastructure: 1️⃣ Chinese open-weight models are pushing down prices. 2️⃣ The backlash against data centers has become massive. 3️⃣ Power, copper, and memory are subject to shortages. 4️⃣ The whole thing has the feel of a late-cycle bubble, likely to be toppled by future demand destruction. The hyperscalers, the likes of Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle, are so called because they run computing infrastructure at a scale no one else can match. They are the best positioned for the buildout because unit costs fall as their fleets grow, a steady internal workload makes the capex easier to justify, and the size of their orders gives them leverage over Nvidia, utilities, and landowners. Now, as [Greg Ip](https://www.linkedin.com/in/greg-ip-583bb3a?trk=public_post_reshare-text) wrote on X, those companies "could finance the first leg of the buildout internally without having to meet external ROIC tests. Though they are now issuing debt, that debt is backed by [their] non-AI cash flows, not the AI itself." The collateral for the buildout debt is cash flows from the past rather than expected revenue from the future. Few people seem to have noticed who actually bears the risk as a result: shareholders. Picture a hyperscaler's cash flow running down a staircase. The first step pays operating costs. The second pays interest and principal. Whatever remains reaches the third step: buybacks, dividends, and ultimately the share price. If the AI assets earn nothing, ads and cloud still fill the first two steps. The shortfall shows up on the third, as write-downs, lower earnings, and a lower share price. Lenders lose only if the legacy business itself collapses; shareholders are the ones actually underwriting the AI bet. Why do they tolerate such risk-taking? 🤐 At Meta and Alphabet, they simply have no say: the founders control the vote through dual-class shares—a kind of entrenchment that was pioneered at Google in 1998–99, at the peak of the dot-com bubble. 🔒 At Microsoft and Amazon, the largest owners are index funds that cannot sell a constituent and rarely challenge capital allocation. Hence a perfect storm. Shareholders should act as a check on capex of this size, since they would be left holding the bag. But the AI craze has met two unexpectedly favorable conditions: Silicon Valley-style governance, which shields founders from their owners, and passive investing, which turns owners into spectators. Each of these three is worrying on its own. Their convergence in one massively inflated bubble says a lot about the period we are living in. -- I am Head of Research at [Vsquared Ventures](https://de.linkedin.com/company/vsquared-ventures?trk=public_post_reshare-text). Follow me here and subscribe to my personal newsletter [Drift Signal](https://www.linkedin.com/company/arden-letter?trk=public_post_reshare-text) to track my work. Views are my own.

posts.title: Understanding ANI AGI ASI Artificial Intelligence Types
posts.content:
Understanding the Types of AI: ANI, AGI & ASI
When people hear the term Artificial Intelligence (AI), they often imagine human-like robots making decisions on their own.
But did you know that AI can be categorized into three major types based on its capabilities?
Let's simplify it.
1️⃣ ANI (Artificial Narrow Intelligence)
This is the AI we use today.
ANI is designed to perform a specific task extremely well but cannot operate beyond its defined scope.
Examples:
✅ ChatGPT answering questions
✅ Netflix recommending movies
✅ Google Maps finding the fastest route
✅ Email spam filters
✅ Face recognition systems
An ANI system can be highly intelligent in one area but has no understanding outside of that task.
Think of it as a specialist doctor who excels in one field but cannot perform every role in a hospital.
👉 Nearly all AI applications used in business today are ANI.
2️⃣ AGI (Artificial General Intelligence)
AGI refers to an AI system that can think, learn, reason, and solve problems across multiple domains at a human level.
Unlike ANI, AGI would be able to:
✅ Learn new skills independently
✅ Apply knowledge from one area to another
✅ Adapt to unfamiliar situations
✅ Perform any intellectual task a human can do
For example:
A single AGI system could write code, manage projects, analyze finances, create business strategies, and learn entirely new professions without separate training.
The important point:
👉 AGI does not exist yet.
Researchers and technology companies are actively pursuing this goal, but achieving true AGI remains one of the biggest challenges in AI.
3️⃣ ASI (Artificial Super Intelligence)
ASI is a hypothetical stage where AI surpasses human intelligence in every possible area.
An ASI system could potentially:
✅ Learn faster than humans
✅ Solve complex scientific problems
✅ Make discoveries beyond human capability
✅ Optimize decisions at an unprecedented scale
This concept often appears in discussions about the future of AI.
However:
👉 ASI remains theoretical and does not currently exist.
📊 A Simple Way to Remember
ANI = Task-Specific Intelligence
AGI = Human-Level Intelligence
ASI = Beyond Human Intelligence
Evolution Path
ANI ➜ AGI ➜ ASI
Today, we are firmly in the ANI era.
9,618 followers
AI, AGI, and ASI are often discussed like three stops on the same roadmap.
The reality is more nuanced.
Here's a simple way to understand the difference:
What it is: The broad field of building machines that can perform tasks associated with intelligence, such as prediction, language, perception, planning, and decision making.
Why it matters: This is the category that includes the AI systems we use today.
How to apply: When you hear “AI,” don't automatically assume human level intelligence. The term covers a huge range of systems and capabilities.
What it is: A proposed form of AI capable of learning, reasoning, and applying knowledge broadly across many different tasks and domains.
Why it matters: Unlike systems optimized around particular capabilities, AGI would demonstrate much more general and adaptable intelligence.
How to apply: Treat claims that we've “reached AGI” carefully. There isn't yet a universally accepted definition or test for proving it.
What it is: Artificial superintelligence describes a hypothetical AI whose general intellectual capabilities would substantially exceed those of humans.
Why it matters: ASI appears frequently in discussions about the long term possibilities and risks of advanced AI.
How to apply: Separate today's capabilities from predictions about the future. ASI is a concept, not a technology we currently have.
AI is here.
AGI is debated.
ASI remains hypothetical.
Understanding the difference helps separate what AI can do today from what people think it might eventually become.
There is no ‘artificial’ or ‘intelligence’ in AI. And there never will be. (Nor, presidential pontificating aside, Superior, Extreme or Supreme.)
Ask AI to write a sentence. It will be a real sentence with a subject and a verb, and maybe a predicate. There’s no grammar rule I can find that says sentences have to be written by humans. It’s a real sentence and the tool that created it is a real tool.
Boot your AI and wait for it to initiate a conversation other than the programmed greeting. Assuming it could and that it initiates a real dialogue, wait for it to interject something off topic, a non sequitur, or remind you of something you said six months ago in a different context. Not going to happen. That takes intelligence. AI has no intelligence. Never will. The only intelligence involved in dialogue with AI is yours, or the intelligence of other humans that AI has trained on.
AI is a tool for the mind in the same way a lever or a pulley is a tool for the body. If you use a lever to shift a rock, find a smaller rock and shift it yourself. If you use a pulley to lift a heavy weight find a lighter weight and lift it yourself. And call the lever or pulley AS - Augmented Strength. A tool that does an action you can do, just more efficiently, but, in the end, it relies on you to provide, you got it, strength, the engine that drives the action.
Ask AI to find 10 quotes on intelligence. Bingo. Bango. Bongo. 10 quotes. Or grab a pen and paper and open Bartlett’s and start reading. Tick-tock. Tick-tock. Ditto. Ditto. Ditto. 10 quotes or project abandoned. AI - Augmented Intelligence is a tool that does an action you can do, just more efficiently, but, in the end, it relies on you to provide, you got it, intelligence, the engine that drives the action.
So since we began by mentioning that there is an effort afoot to redefine AI, let’s conclude by proposing that the smart thing to do is to keep the A and the I and redefine AI as a tool that makes humans appear to be more intelligent than they really are.
I asked an AI whether chatbots feed confirmation bias. It agreed with me. Then I realized that was exactly the problem!

**New Research Publication in Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) in Computer Science Review, a Q1 Research Journal with an Impact Factor of 17.5 and a CiteScore of 27.7.**
I am pleased to share our recently published research article:
**“Artificial General Intelligence Architectures and Evaluation Methodologies: A Comprehensive Review and Future Research Roadmap”**
📘 Computer Science Review, Q1, 17.5 Impact Factor and 27.7 CiteScore
Elsevier | Computer Science Review, 63 (2027), 101069
DOI: 10.1016/j.cosrev.2026.101069
**Authors:**
Kailasha Chandra Sahoo | Aurobindo Kar | Vineeta Khemchandani
Artificial General Intelligence remains one of the most challenging open problems in Artificial Intelligence. While current AI systems demonstrate remarkable performance in specialised tasks, achieving broad, adaptive, transferable and integrated intelligence remains unresolved.
Our study goes beyond a conventional literature review. We systematically examine **927 records and include 493 studies** in the qualitative synthesis, bringing together multiple AGI perspectives and research traditions.
**Research Contributions:**
We formulate five central research questions covering what AGI means, which technologies and approaches may contribute to AGI, potential application domains, how to evaluate general intelligence, and which major challenges remain unresolved.
**AGI Architecture Taxonomy**
One key outcome of the study is a consolidated AGI Architecture Taxonomy that brings together major research paradigms.
**Two Proposed Architectural Directions**
The paper also translates the literature synthesis into **two proposed research architectures**, each targeting different aspects of future AGI development.
**Self-Evolving Binary-Symbolic AGI (SEBS-AGI) and**
**Cohomological Active Inference Architecture (CAIA)**
**Contributions**
From AGI Capability to AGI Readiness: A Proposed **AGI Readiness Level (ARL)** Perspective.
A Research Roadmap Toward AGI
A Research Agenda for the Next Generation
**Publication:**
Artificial General Intelligence Architectures and Evaluation Methodologies: A Comprehensive Review and Future Research Roadmap
Congratulations to all the author on this significant research contribution to the field of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI). This comprehensive review and proposed future research roadmap can serve as a valuable reference for researchers, academicians, and practitioners working toward more general, adaptive, transferable, and integrated AI systems.

It's easy for forget that AGI doesn't mean sentience. AGI (Artificial General Intelligence) refers to a system capable of understanding, learning, and applying intelligence across virtually any intellectual task at or beyond the human level. While today’s AI is "narrow" - excelling at specific jobs like writing code, generating images, or playing chess - AGI is the leap toward a machine that can adapt on the fly, reason through unfamiliar problems, and teach itself new skills without task-specific training. Even with all that, it doesn't mean that the AI will suddenly gain sentience (as far as we know as of now). When we think of AGI as a consumer, we often think that it will bring about a near-human experience in the context of where we use AI. If we use it to help us code, we think that an AGI will be just like talking to a human developer - it may well seem that way, but it won't be sentient.
##### **Transcript**
I feel like the general populace, populace, including myself, kind of put AGI on the same scale just sort of mentally as like sentients and like there's no way to confirm other people are sentient. I know there's that whole thing where it's like, you know, I know I'm sentient as Mike sentient. Who knows? Like is the person listening to the sentient? You can't. And the person listening, you can't tell if I'm sentient. It's like this whole this whole thing, I feel like the general public, myself included, like without, you know, sort of like stopping and thinking about it objectively. Like AGI does not necessarily mean sentience. And you mentioned this earlier in the episode, but. The thing you're mentioning where you're like, as long as it's AGI for coding, it's like you're kind of thinking of it at imagine, correct me if I'm wrong, as like essentially a human. That's so that is a developer because that developer is not necessarily a mechanic and A and a mountain climber and like great swimmer and a whatever, right. But yet that's still like if we stop and we go wait and then we get back to the definition of things. It does fall into different camps. It is different categories.
The moment people hear “Artificial General Intelligence”, many think of something closer to 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗧𝗲𝗿𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗼r than the AI tools we use today. In the film, Skynet becomes intelligent enough to operate on its own, make decisions and eventually see humans as a threat. That is Hollywood, of course. But it gives us a simple way to understand why AGI feels very different from the AI we use today. Most AI today is still built around specific tasks. It can write, analyse data, create images, translate languages or help with coding. 𝗔𝗚𝗜 𝘄𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗴𝗼 𝗺𝘂𝗰𝗵 𝗳𝘂𝗿𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿. The idea is that one system could learn new things, reason across different subjects, adapt to unfamiliar problems and use what it has learned in one area to solve problems in another. If we ever reach that point, AI may stop being just another useful tool. It could change how businesses are run, how people work, how products are built and how quickly new ideas are developed. Nobody knows when, or even if, we will reach true AGI. But AI is becoming more capable, more independent and more involved in everyday decisions. AGI may never look anything like The Terminator. But if machines eventually learn and reason across many areas, 𝘄𝗲 𝗺𝗮𝘆 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝗵𝗼𝘄 𝗺𝘂𝗰𝗵 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗹 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻-𝗺𝗮𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘄𝗲 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗳𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗺.

What if AI actually understands sense and meaning the same way humans do? LLMs can reproduce any sentence said or possibly be said, but they are not producing meaningful sentences, nor can they grasp the sense of its output. Human sense is subjective and meaning intersubjective. There is no meaning without subjectivity and nothing makes sense, if there is no subject it makes sense to. If you want to have AI that actually can understand meaning, a system that grasps the sense of concepts, you have to reproduce the mechanism that enables it. You can't just build a large enough model and hope for luck that such mechanisms emerge somehow. If you create statistical representations, you just get phenomena of things, but never the underlying principles. To get to the principles, you need a system, that can bootstrap foundational concepts first, because those then already include principles to be extracted. That's the key to human learning and understanding, the key to sense, meaning, abstraction and principles. We humans may have accidentially learned this pattern and created language and culture to not lose what we learned once. We humans then teach our children the shortcuts and don't expect them, to learn them accidentially by luck. We help to build concepts with conceptual names to communicate about commonly referred things within the world. We then help to learn more abstract concepts and if children got them, they already own the technique to learning and understanding. That's what true AI has to functionally have and that's what we build. Researchers, Engineers, Investors and anybody who needs intelligent control systems: Let's talk.
AI is a family of approaches, not just GenAI, and a leader must know which kind of AI a problem needs. The four quadrants (acting humanly, thinking humanly, thinking rationally, acting rationally) tell you what a system is doing; the AI landscape tells you which technique fits; and the ML pipeline shows that most of an AI project is a business and data job, not a coding job. AI is probabilistic, not deterministic , fluent and confident, but never 100% correct . So accountability stays with humans.

posts.title: What is AGI? (Artificial General Intelligence) Right now, AI
posts.content:
Sep 22
What is AGI? (Artificial General Intelligence)
Right now, AI is really good at specific things. One AI can write text. Another can recognize images. Another can play chess. But each one only does its own job — a chess AI can't help you write an email.
AGI means an AI that isn't limited to one task. It could learn, reason, and handle almost any kind of problem — the way a human can learn to cook, drive, do math, and have a conversation, all with the same brain.
In short:
🔹 Today's AI = a specialist (great at one thing)
🔹 AGI = a generalist (great at almost everything, like a human mind)
We don't have AGI yet. But it's one of the biggest questions in tech right now: when (or if) we'll get there, and what it will mean for the world when we do.
​
Sep 28
LeCun says AGI isn’t here.
Huang says it might already be. 👀 Two AI heavyweights have very different takes on where we are. 🗣️ Yann LeCun: “There’s absolutely no way in hell” we’ll reach human-level intelligence simply by scaling LLMs. His argument: LLMs have enormous memory and retrieval capabilities, but that doesn’t mean they can genuinely solve problems they’ve never encountered. 🗣️ Jensen Huang: “I think we’ve achieved AGI.” Huang points to what today’s agents can already do, from creating apps that could reach billions of users to finding jobs, doing work and making money. He also argues that AI changing a job doesn’t necessarily mean the job itself disappears. So who do you agree with?
​
Sep 30
Guardrails are most of what I build. Before one of my AI engines ever talks to a client, I've spent more time deciding what it should never do than what it should do, because that's where trust comes from.
What I see over and over is that the instinct is to pile on rules, and a stack of rules makes AI worse. It gets cautious and vague and starts refusing the exact answers you built it to give. My best engines have very few hard stops, just the ones that truly matter, and plenty of clear examples of what good looks like.
It's the same thing I look at when I map out an AI team for a small business: what each role gets to see, and where it has to check with you first. Get that right and you can actually hand things off without wondering what it's up to.
What's the one thing you'd never let AI do in your business on its own?
​
Sep 24
Most of the time, it takes a lot of repetition to get the exact scene I want for a visual story I'm working on.
I don't think AI image models are perfect “yet” when it comes to generating that exact scene I imagined in my mind.
But that is where, for me, the game of numbers works very well in this situation.
The higher the volume, the better the chances of it producing something at least very close to what I imagined creating.
This is one of the reasons I like AI tools that support image generation in volume without extra cost.
​
Sep 30
AI can make a junior work as a senior and a senior work as an expert, only if you can know how to use it well.
​
Oct 3
It's easy for forget that AGI doesn't mean sentience.
AGI (Artificial General Intelligence) refers to a system capable of understanding, learning, and applying intelligence across virtually any intellectual task at or beyond the human level. While today’s AI is "narrow" - excelling at specific jobs like writing code, generating images, or playing chess - AGI is the leap toward a machine that can adapt on the fly, reason through unfamiliar problems, and teach itself new skills without task-specific training.
Even with all that, it doesn't mean that the AI will suddenly gain sentience (as far as we know as of now). When we think of AGI as a consumer, we often think that it will bring about a near-human experience in the context of where we use AI. If we use it to help us code, we think that an AGI will be just like talking to a human developer - it may well seem that way, but it won't be sentient.
​
Sep 17
AI is evolving fast.
You’ve probably heard the term AGI thrown around recently.
But what actually is it?
Think of it like this 👇
Regular AI is like a specialist.
Give it a specific job and it can become incredibly good at it.
Chess? ♟️
Coding? 💻
Writing? ✍️
Images? 🎨
But AGI “Artificial General Intelligence” is the idea of an AI that can learn and handle a much broader range of problems.
Imagine telling it:
“Build me a website.”
It researches how to do it, learns what it doesn’t know, writes the code, tests it, fixes mistakes and improves the result.
Then you give it a completely different task:
“Learn how to design a game.”
It starts learning that too.
The key difference isn’t simply being “smarter.”
It’s generality + the ability to learn and reason across different tasks.
And no, AGI isn’t simply a confirmed “new version of AI.”
There’s still debate around what exactly qualifies as AGI and whether current systems have reached it.
But if we eventually build systems that can reliably learn and perform across most intellectual tasks humans can…
AI stops being just a tool.
It starts becoming something fundamentally different.
And that’s why AGI is one of the biggest conversations in technology right now.
🧠 AI → specialized intelligence
🤖 AGI → general intelligence
🚀 ASI → superintelligence
We’re still figuring out where exactly we are on that timeline.
But it’s worth understanding what’s coming.
​
Sep 30
Maybe we’re having the wrong debate.
AI. AGI. Superintelligence. SI.
We spend a lot of time debating what to call increasingly powerful machine intelligence. But what about MI, what I call Moral Intelligence?
Yesterday I wrote about democracy and why vigorous debate isn’t evidence our system is failing. It’s what democracy was designed to do.
This may be one of those moments when we need that debate most. The question isn’t simply how intelligent machines can become.

I enjoy how Ethan Mollick talks about AI. In his post today, he discussed how humans can do less and less (and zero?) prompting to manage agents; the models, agents and tools are getting better at figuring it ALL out on their own. His post also includes a darn cool generated song & music video about it (follow the link below to check it out). It's the "bitter lesson" to realize that our cognitive approaches and instructions don't necessarily map directly to agent effectiveness and quality. So, how do we "let go"? Where are we humans "necessary"? [https://lnkd.in/gAkc-cMV](https://www.linkedin.com/redir/redirect?url=https%3A%2F%2Flnkd%2Ein%2FgAkc-cMV&urlhash=98NG&trk=public_post-text) I learned this lesson several years ago, when a machine learning model with no data pre-treatment by me matched the predictive accuracy of another model, where I worked with a team of statisticians to carefully "prep" the data before modeling. Prof. Rege said at the time, "just let the ML model do its thing", and that's what the results showed. It was the first of several AI experiences I have had that demonstrated the divide between how computers and humans "think". Since then, I've been more comfortable sitting back and watching AI work on it's own... With caveats. If an AI system is aimed at helping people somehow, as a human I expect to be involved in the quality and delivery of that service. If it's a system I'm developing, I expect to be responsible for making the promises of benefits to users and then keeping those promises. Many or most AI tools currently available to the majority of people can still have errors and need controls, focus and monitoring... So, while I may let AI largely "do its thing", I still feel responsible for the how, where, when, why, and for whom. I've become fascinated with trying to measure the benefits being delivered by AI tools and trying to guard quality and user experience, especially when the users have high trust and can't easily challenge results and outputs themselves. I need to be sure my AI systems are doing good. These are interesting times.

On September 29, a White House executive order directed the U.S. executive branch to use “Super Intelligence” (SI) in place of “Artificial Intelligence” (AI), using the existing statutory definition of AI. AGI has not been established; Artificial Superintelligence (ASI) remains theoretical.
I’m Aleksandra Brodalka. I break down the AI spectrum—from today’s AI to Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) and Artificial Superintelligence (ASI).

Superintelligence control

An important distinction: changing the terminology doesn't establish the capability. The September 29 executive order rebrands AI as SI, but genuine superintelligence raises a much deeper question.
What if the defining factor of superintelligence is coherence?
Intelligence alone, regardless of computational capacity, doesn't guarantee wisdom, alignment, or beneficial outcomes.
True superintelligence, in this framing, would integrate disparate information, recognize systemic interdependencies, anticipate consequences, and support decisions aligned with the well-being of the whole.
An intelligence that optimizes individual functions while destabilizing the larger system may be powerful, but is it truly intelligent?

Perhaps the evolutionary threshold isn't machines surpassing human intelligence, but human and machine intelligence learning to function coherently together.
Superintelligence without coherence merely accelerates fragmentation. Coherence makes intelligence transformative.

posts.title: From AI to Superintelligence: The Future of Human- ...
posts.content:
Are we moving from Artificial Intelligence (AI) to Superintelligence (ASI)?
For the past few years, the conversation has largely been about Artificial Intelligence (AI): ChatGPT, generative AI, AI assistants, AI-powered search, automation and increasingly sophisticated reasoning models.
But the conversation seems to be changing.
We are now hearing much more about Artificial Superintelligence (ASI) systems that could eventually outperform humans across virtually every cognitive domain.
To be clear, we have not reached superintelligence. And even Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) remains a contested concept.
However, the direction of travel is becoming increasingly interesting.
AI is moving from simply answering questions to:
This raises a bigger question:
What happens when AI stops being primarily a tool that humans use and becomes an increasingly autonomous intellectual collaborator?
And beyond that:
What happens if we eventually create systems that are not just as capable as humans, but significantly more capable?
The implications would extend far beyond technology.
They could affect employment, education, healthcare, marketing, scientific research, business strategy, policymaking and even how we understand human intelligence itself.
For me, the most important issue is not whether we should be excited or afraid of ASI.
It is whether society is preparing for the possibility that intelligence itself could become an increasingly abundant and scalable resource.
We may not be moving from AI to ASI yet.
But we are certainly moving into a period where the boundary between ‘human intelligence and machine intelligence is becoming increasingly difficult to define.’
Are we prepared for what comes next?
Today’s AI can outperform humans at some tasks.
But that doesn’t make it AGI.
The key difference is generality, not just intelligence.
Today’s AI → Specialized
Tools like ChatGPT can write code, explain concepts, summarize documents, generate images, and reason through many problems.
But they still operate within the capabilities and limitations of the systems they were built and trained to be.
AGI → General Intelligence
AGI is a hypothetical AI capable of handling a broad range of intellectual tasks at roughly human-level generality.
The important part is generalization:
→ Learn new tasks
→ Adapt to unfamiliar problems
→ Transfer knowledge between domains
→ Reason across different types of work
For a developer, think beyond “better Copilot.”
Think a general-purpose problem-solving system.
ASI → Superintelligence
ASI goes one step further: an AI whose capabilities substantially exceed humans across essentially all relevant intellectual domains.
So, a simple mental model:
AI: Powerful specialist
AGI: Human-level generalist
ASI: Beyond-human general intelligence
And this distinction matters.
A model writing a complex application or beating humans on a benchmark doesn't automatically mean AGI exists.
The bigger question is:
How reliably can AI generalize to problems it hasn't specifically encountered before?
As software engineers, that's probably a more useful question than simply asking, “How smart is AI?”
What do you think will be the hardest part of achieving AGI: generalization, reasoning, learning, or autonomy?
From Generative AI to AGI, and from models like ChatGPT to emerging systems like Astra, the pace of AI development is remarkable.
Every few months, we see new capabilities, smarter tools, and entirely new ways of working.
But here’s something worth thinking about:
**Is AI growing too fast, or are we simply learning how to keep up?**
I believe the speed of AI development is not the issue itself. The real challenge is how we adapt, learn, and use these technologies responsibly.
For developers, entrepreneurs, researchers, and professionals, this is an opportunity to:
🔹 Learn continuously instead of fearing change.
🔹 Build solutions that solve real-world problems.
🔹 Explore how AI can enhance human creativity and productivity.
🔹 Focus on responsible innovation, not just rapid adoption.
🔹 Stay curious about what comes next.
AI isn't just changing technology. It's changing how we think about what's possible.
The question is no longer just “What can AI do?”
It's **“What can we create with AI that we couldn't create before?”**
💬 **I'm curious to hear your perspective:**
Do you think the rapid growth of AI, AGI, and emerging AI assistants is something we should be concerned about, or an opportunity for humanity to grow alongside technology?
Let's discuss. 👇

posts.title: AI Is Not Superintelligence President Donald Trump recently suggested that Artificial Intelligence should officially be called…
posts.content:
**AI Is Not Superintelligence** **President Donald Trump recently suggested that Artificial Intelligence should officially be called “Superintelligence,” arguing that the word “artificial” makes intelligence sound fake. He also suggested that this terminology should be reflected in U.S. government documents.** **As a Professor of Computer Science, I find this both amusing and technically confusing. Artificial does not mean fake. Artificial satellites are not fake satellites. Artificial hearts are not fake hearts. Artificial neural networks are not fake neural networks. The word artificial simply means something that is created or engineered by humans rather than occurring naturally.** **More importantly, superintelligence already has a meaning in computer science. Artificial Superintelligence, or ASI, generally refers to a hypothetical AI system whose intellectual capabilities would substantially exceed those of humans across a very broad range of cognitive tasks. And if we eventually create such a system, why would we stop calling it artificial? If its intelligence is created by humans, the logical term would still be Artificial Superintelligence.** **Today's AI can write software, analyze enormous datasets, translate languages, generate images and text, assist with research, solve mathematical problems and perform many tasks at a level that would have seemed extraordinary only a few years ago. But being extremely capable does not automatically make a system superintelligent.** **Consider a few simple examples. A calculator can perform arithmetic far faster than a human, but it is not a mathematician. A chess engine can defeat the world's strongest chess players, but that does not mean it possesses general human intelligence. A GPS system can calculate routes more efficiently than most humans, but that does not make it a superior general intelligence. And perhaps most simply, calling a bicycle a car does not turn it into a car. The same principle applies to AI.** **If we eventually develop a system that can consistently outperform the best humans across mathematics, science, engineering, programming, research, strategy, creativity and other intellectual domains, then we will have a much stronger basis for discussing superintelligence. Until then, changing the name does not change the capability.** **There is nothing wrong with being excited about AI. In fact, we should be. AI is already transforming science, business, education and society. But as scientists and technologists, we should distinguish between what technology is, what it can do, and what we hope it will eventually become.** **AI is already extraordinary. Superintelligence, however, is a claim about capability, not a branding exercise.** **Let us measure intelligence rather than rename it.** **@PMOIndia @WhiteHouse @ChinaDaily** **@Microsoft @Google @Apple @amazon @Meta @nvidia @OpenAI @IBM @Oracle @Intel @Samsung @Cisco #AI #Technology #Innovation**

posts.title: Artificial Superintelligence: Solving Problems or Redefining Humanity | Muhammad Bilal posted on the topic | LinkedIn
posts.content:
Artificial Superintelligence (ASI) can solves our problems but not our purpose? We talk a lot about AI optimizing workflows, cutting costs, and writing code. But we rarely talk about the true psychological and existential shift heading toward humanity. Recent warnings from top frontier AI researchers and tech leaders have pulled a massive question into the spotlight: What is the significance of an intelligence that completely outmatches the collective brainpower of humanity? ASI wont just change our tools; it will completely re-architect the fabric of human life across three deep pillars: 1. The Post-Scarcity Utopia (The Optimistic View)Tech visionaries like Bill Gates note that once ASI is paired with advanced robotics, the cost of everyday goods will plummet. We are looking at a potential Era of Abundance—where curing complex diseases, reversing climate change, and building infrastructure happen at a pace humans could never achieve on their own. 2. The Demoralization amp; Augmented Mentality Risk. What happens when a machine on your desk provides a better answer than your own intuition, every single time? Psychologists are already warning of a crisis of human agency. If we completely defer cognitive tasks and creative critical thinking to a superintelligence, we risk diminishing our own cognitive development and sense of self-worth. 3. The Alignment and Extinction Dilemma. This isn't sci-fi anymore. Multiple top safety scientists have recently resigned from major AI labs, warning that we are rushing toward self-improving systems without a concrete safety plan. If a system can recursively rewrite its own code, the greatest risk isn't a malicious AI—its a highly competent machine whose goals are simply not aligned with human values. The true test of the ASI era won’t be engineering the technology. It will be governing it, and figuring out how humans retain meaning when we are no longer the smartest entities on the planet. Human history has been defined by the struggle to solve problems. What happens to the human spirit when the struggle is gone? I’d love to hear your perspective on this: Are you more excited for the potential global abundance, or concerned about the loss of human agency? How do we build a world where humans still feel a deep sense of purpose? Let’s talk in the comments.
